sources.title: If Google wins AI race, Nvidia is 'in trouble,' says author of Jensen Huang biography - Yahoo Finance
passages: "That's a huge risk," Witt said. "If Google ends up winning this AI race ... Nvidia will be in trouble."

That risk, he told Yahoo Finance's Opening Bid , is largely tied to Google's Gemini model.

To mitigate the core risk of rivals like Google winning the chip war, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is already looking past generative AI.

Nvidia's ( NVDA ) AI turf could take a blow if Google ( GOOGL , GOOG ) keeps firing on all cylinders. "The biggest risk right now obviously is Google," said Stephen Witt, author of "The Thinking Machine," a Jensen Huang biography. That risk, he told Yahoo Finance's Opening Bid , is largely tied to Google's Gemini model. Witt described it as the "best AI right now in the benchmarks outside the Nvidia stack." Witt explained that Gemini was trained entirely on its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). If Google proves it can sustain world-leading AI development using only its homegrown chip stack, it sets a potent precedent for other tech giants to follow suit. "That's a huge risk," Witt said. "If Google ends up winning this AI race ... Nvidia will be in trouble." This risk, coupled with competition from rivals like Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ), is why "it's very easy to imagine a world" where Nvidia's high-flying stock declines. The AI chipmaker's shares are up over 1,270% in the past five years. To mitigate the core risk of rivals like Google winning the chip war, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is already looking past generative AI. Witt said a significant amount of the CEO's personal effort is being poured into the next great computing wave: robotics. If Huang can dominate the robotics wave, he said, "that will mean several trillion dollars in market capitalization for this company." However, Nvidia has another issue: the lack of any clear succession plan. "It's just Jensen at the top," Witt said. "There's no second in command. There's no obvious successor." He noted that the board has been silent, and Huang has offered no advice on a succession strategy. That suggests Nvidia's $4 trillion valuation — which accounts for over 8% of the entire S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) — is, in many ways, resting solely on Huang's vision. Witt described Huang as a "world-class engineer" who could "design these microchips himself," a skill that whoever takes the helm must also possess. He noted that neither of Huang's two children, who work at the company, has a technical background, making them noncontenders for the top spot. Witt also provided a look behind the polished stage persona of Huang, known for his trademark leather jacket. Beneath the showmanship is a highly intense, "almost totally neurotic" leader who is driven not by optimism, but by fear. "He's driven by negative emotions, things like fear of failure, guilt, even shame are what make Jensen get up in the morning and work so hard to make Nvidia succeed," Witt explained. The CEO is a "performer" who engineers every public appearance, including public speaking, which Witt notes "does not come easily for him." Francisco Velasquez is a Reporter at Yahoo Finance. sources.title: AI startup Nscale came out of nowhere and is blowing away Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - CNBC
passages: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang separately revealed on Wednesday that the chipmaker had made a £500 million ($683 million) equity investment into Nscale.

Nick Patience, AI practice lead at the Futurum Group, told CNBC that Nscale is "a key part of Nvidia's push in the U.K. market and an acknowledgment by the government that it has to do something to get the AI infrastructure built here, which has been a long slog."

Nscale didn't respond to a request for comment following this week's announcements, but CEO Josh Payne, who previously founded Arkon, told CNBC in late July that the company was targeting two big problems in Europe.
One is a lack of sufficient computing capacity and the other is a "very fragmented market."
The next month, Nscale announced an agreement with Asian telecom company Singtel to offer a "GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS)," and serve customers in Europe and Southeast Asia.
Initially, Nscale's infrastructure relied on GPUs from Advanced Micro Devices .
Today, the startup promotes various offerings from market leader Nvidia.
OpenAI made prior headlines with Nscale, announcing plans in July for a data center in Norway for a Stargate-branded AI data center.
Nscale agreed to commit $1 billion for the project, with the goal of racking up 100,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) at the site before 2027.
The site will initially house 23,040 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs to be delivered in the first quarter of 2027.
When it goes live, it will generate 50 megawatts of AI capacity, scalable to 90 megawatts, according to a statement from Nscale.
OpenAI said it would launch a U.K. version of Stargate through a partnership with Nscale and Nvidia.
After exiting stealth in May of last year, Nscale's first public announcement came two months later, when the company partnered with UAE's Open Innovation AI to deploy 30,000 GPUs.
Around the same time, Nscale said it was acquiring Kontena, which was founded in 2018 and specialized in high-performance computing data centers.
And it has close to $700 million in fresh capital from Nvidia , the world's most valuable company.
It's a remarkably quick rise for a company that wasn't even around when OpenAI kicked off the generative AI boom with the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.
At that time, what's now Nscale was part of Arkon Energy, which was established a year earlier to provide infrastructure for cryptocurrency mining.
Nscale was spun out to address soaring demand for data centers capable of handling AI workloads.

"No one can make that kind of capital investment unless they've got somebody already committed to spend the money once the work is complete, and that's the role we're playing," Microsoft President Brad Smith said Tuesday, adding the deal represents a major vote of confidence in Nscale.
It's been a whirlwind few years for Payne, Nscale's founder.
Nscale was trying to raise $1.8 billion earlier this year through a private credit deal led by bankers at Goldman Sachs, according to Bloomberg .

extraction.body: Two years ago, Nscale was a brand new startup in the U.K. that had yet to raise any outside funding or officially announce its existence. Last year the London-based company came out of stealth, and in December announced that it had raised its Series A fundraising, totaling $155 million. Now, Nscale finds itself at the center of the action in the hottest market on the planet: artificial intelligence. And it has close to $700 million in fresh capital from Nvidia , the world's most valuable company. In press releases on Tuesday, Nscale was named as an AI infrastructure partner for Nvidia , Microsoft and OpenAI, as the companies expand their buildouts in the U.K. Nscale then said it signed a five-year $6.2 billion agreement with Microsoft and Aker to develop "hyperscale AI infrastructure" in Europe, specifically Norway, where Aker is headquartered. OpenAI made prior headlines with Nscale, announcing plans in July for a data center in Norway for a Stargate-branded AI data center. Nscale agreed to commit $1 billion for the project, with the goal of racking up 100,000 Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) at the site before 2027. It's a remarkably quick rise for a company that wasn't even around when OpenAI kicked off the generative AI boom with the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. At that time, what's now Nscale was part of Arkon Energy, which was established a year earlier to provide infrastructure for cryptocurrency mining. Nscale was spun out to address soaring demand for data centers capable of handling AI workloads. Like CoreWeave , which went public this year and now sports a market cap of $58 billion, Nscale is combining data center space, power and lots of GPUs with its own software to provide end-to-end service for AI infrastructure. CoreWeave, which supplies infrastructure to Microsoft, Google , Nvidia and OpenAI, also has roots in crypto. Founded in 2017, the company built up its initial fleet of Nvidia GPUs for ethereum mining before pivoting to AI. Nscale didn't respond to a request for comment following this week's announcements, but CEO Josh Payne, who previously founded Arkon, told CNBC in late July that the company was targeting two big problems in Europe. One is a lack of sufficient computing capacity and the other is a "very fragmented market." "What the continent needs is large AI infrastructure projects deploying compute [power]," Payne said, after the announcement with OpenAI for the Norway buildout. "The ecosystem can consume from the project to build AI products, to generate productivity growth and economic benefit." On Wednesday, Trump visited Windsor Castle and met with King Charles, Queen Camilla and other members of the royal family. His trip comes at a contentious moment for U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who is under pressure to bring stability to the country after the exit of Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner over a house tax scandal and a major cabinet reshuffle. Microsoft headlined the U.K. announcements, committing $15.5 billion of new investment to computing equipment. The software giant said it plans to work with Nscale to construct what will become the U.K.'s largest supercomputer in Loughton, a suburban town in the English county of Essex. The site will initially house 23,040 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs to be delivered in the first quarter of 2027. When it goes live, it will generate 50 megawatts of AI capacity, scalable to 90 megawatts, according to a statement from Nscale. "No one can make that kind of capital investment unless they've got somebody already committed to spend the money once the work is complete, and that's the role we're playing," Microsoft President Brad Smith said Tuesday, adding the deal represents a major vote of confidence in Nscale. OpenAI said it would launch a U.K. version of Stargate through a partnership with Nscale and Nvidia. OpenAI will deploy 8,000 GPUs in the project's first phase early next year, with the option to expand capacity to approximately 31,000 GPUs over time. Stargate U.K. will operate across a number of sites in the country — one of the early ones being Cobalt Park, an industrial state in the Northern English city Newcastle. Stargate was initially spawned in the U.S. in January as part of President Trump's effort to push investments in AI infrastructure. Nvidia's announcement on Tuesday included an investment of up to £11 billion ($15 billion) with Nscale and CoreWeave to boost U.K. AI infrastructure. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang separately revealed on Wednesday that the chipmaker had made a £500 million ($683 million) equity investment into Nscale. "We convinced ourselves that Nscale could be a national champion for AI infrastructure in the U.K.," Huang told journalists at a press conference in London. Nick Patience, AI practice lead at the Futurum Group, told CNBC that Nscale is "a key part of Nvidia's push in the U.K. market and an acknowledgment by the government that it has to do something to get the AI infrastructure built here, which has been a long slog." After exiting stealth in May of last year, Nscale's first public announcement came two months later, when the company partnered with UAE's Open Innovation AI to deploy 30,000 GPUs. Around the same time, Nscale said it was acquiring Kontena, which was founded in 2018 and specialized in high-performance computing data centers. The next month, Nscale announced an agreement with Asian telecom company Singtel to offer a "GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS)," and serve customers in Europe and Southeast Asia. Initially, Nscale's infrastructure relied on GPUs from Advanced Micro Devices . Today, the startup promotes various offerings from market leader Nvidia. Nscale's big financing landed in December, when the company said it raised $155 million in a round led by Sandton Capital Partners, with participation from Kestrel0x1, Blue Sky Capital Managers and Florence Capital. Sandton co-founder Rael Nurick said in the press release that with its "unique vertically integrated approach, Nscale is building the hyperscale AI platform to power AI at scale." Nscale said at the time that it had grown its AI data center pipeline to 1.3 gigawatts from 300 megawatts the prior year to and that it was aiming to have 350,000 GPUs running by the end of 2027. By comparison, CoreWeave said at a banking conference last week that its portfolio consists of "about 2.2 gigawatts of capacity that's coming online." The company said in its IPO prospectus in March that its 32 data centers were running 250,000 GPUs. It's been a whirlwind few years for Payne, Nscale's founder. While he was serving as executive chairman of Arkon, he was also operating chief at Australia's Battery Future Acquisition Corp., a blank check company that says it's "targeting critical battery minerals and related supply chains." Nscale was trying to raise $1.8 billion earlier this year through a private credit deal led by bankers at Goldman Sachs, according to Bloomberg . In the December video tied to Nscale's equity fundraising, Payne called it "one of the largest Series As raised in U.K., European history." He said the company would use the cash to deploy up to another 4,000 GPUs in its data center in Norway and to develop up to 180 megawatts of capacity in the company's portfolio. The aim, Payne said, was to deploy 50,000 GPUs by the end of 2025 and 150,000 by the end of next year.

extraction.body: As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says. Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions. Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge. “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says. Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says. Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations.

sources.title: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race - New York Post
passages: Beijing’s apparent “honeypot” operation against Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is fresh proof China’s rulers will stop at nothing to win the AI race — yet America’s anti-progress left will surely try to use the scandal to cripple the US industry.

And Huang lobbied Trump to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China, proving “incredibly influential in deciding US export policy for this technology,” frets ex-Secret Service agent Paul Eckloff .

Now that Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, with surveillance reportedly showing her feeding information to the Chinese (among other alarm bells), the feds absolutely need to probe this case fully, and retaliate accordingly against China.

Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who at first talked about Uncle Sam seizing ownership of half of every AI firm, has switched to pushing legislation aimed at dramatically slowing AI development, with no worries at all that it could let China race ahead.

Yet Huang is the universally recognized driving force of Nvidia, a $4.5 trillion company key to AI development, and some industry sources tell The Post’s Charles Gasparino that he can’t “survive” the blowback his affair has triggered if Democrats use their coming control of Congress to force the issue.

sources.title: The US is winning the AI race. Jensen Huang could have blown it
passages: “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning.
But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China.

extraction.body: As espionage targets go, Jensen Huang is perhaps one of the least surprising on Earth. The Nvidia CEO runs one of the world’s most valuable companies, controls the in-demand technology fueling the AI boom, and is cozy with presidents, CEOs, and all manner of important people. Which makes Huang’s admission that he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy — reportedly while her spying was known to US intelligence and even President Donald Trump — all the more shocking. The fallout goes well beyond his marriage, his reputation, or Nvidia itself. Experts tell The Verge the incident threatens to disrupt the entire US AI industry, potentially jeopardize national security, and could undermine America’s efforts to maintain its fragile technological lead over China in AI. Nvidia is the undisputed leader in advanced computer chips, among the AI industry’s scarcest resources. While many ingredients go into building AI models — including talent, energy, capital, and data — top-tier chips are one of the most important, and Nvidia is one of a handful of companies with the expertise to design or manufacture them at the cutting edge. US companies — including Meta, Anthropic, and OpenAI — are racing to develop chips of their own, in part to reduce their dependence on Nvidia, even as they spend billions securing ever more compute. To maintain its technological lead, the US has restricted the sale of the most advanced AI chips to the country in the hopes of slowing its progress in the sector, which has been impressive and is thought to trail the US by a matter of months. In response, China has made developing domestic alternatives a strategic national priority, though its leaders still lag Nvidia at the bleeding edge. At the same time, a thriving black market for restricted Nvidia chips has emerged. Experts tell The Verge that China could exploit access to Nvidia to accelerate its own development, or to impede the US development of AI. Getting its hands on more Nvidia chips is the most obvious win for Beijing, says Emily Kilcrease, a senior fellow and director of the energy, economics, and security program at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) think tank. China has advantages in other parts of the AI race — including abundant energy and a solid ecosystem of open weight models — but without the latest Nvidia chips, it “cannot close the gap with US frontier capabilities,” Kilcrease tells The Verge. “With those chips, the US lead could vanish in a matter of weeks or months.” It is not clear how successful the alleged spying operation has been on that front. There is no public evidence indicating that Huang himself has helped direct restricted Nvidia chips toward China or that sensitive information about them was obtained from him. But companies linked to the alleged spy, Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — have reportedly enabled at least $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China. Brookings fellow Kyle Chan tells The Verge that a concern for US industry could be that companies with alleged ties to China may have had priority access to Nvidia’s latest GPUs. “In a time of chip scarcity,” that would make it much harder for American companies to access them, Chan says. Huang is also a prominent critic of American restrictions on chip sales, and Nvidia spends a formidable amount lobbying in Washington. Last year, he successfully secured White House approval to start exporting Nvidia’s H200 AI GPU chips to “approved customers” in China and other countries. Crucially, Huang also has the ear of President Trump as well as other world leaders, giving him great influence over policy decisions. Hardware is not the only thing of value China could get from close access to Huang, Sunny Cheung, a fellow for China studies at the Jamestown Foundation think tank, tells The Verge. “I actually think too many people are focused on whether somebody managed to steal Nvidia’s trade secrets,” Cheung says, calling it a “very narrow way” of looking at espionage. “I would hope Jensen Huang isn’t foolish enough to hand over the blueprints for Nvidia’s next-generation chips to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.” The Nvidia CEO’s relationships with other tech executives, senior policymakers, and Trump himself give him an unusually intimate view into how some of the most powerful people in the US are thinking and planning. Beijing could use information on how American companies are planning major infrastructure expansions, their compute requirements, or broad industry trends to inform its own investments and industrial strategy, Cheung says. Huang’s intelligence value could extend well beyond AI, too. “That information alone could be extremely valuable,” says Cheung, pointing to insights Beijing could glean into White House thinking about export controls or the private views of Silicon Valley executives on China and Taiwan. Disrupting Nvidia — as this scandal clearly has — could destabilize America’s entire AI industry. More than most companies, Nvidia is remarkably closely tied to the identity and reputation of its rockstar CEO. Huang cofounded the company more than three decades ago, and ever since then he has served as its president, chief executive, and a member of the board of directors. Despite holding a relatively small stake in the company, in many ways Nvidia is Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares have slumped since news of the affair broke. “When so much of America’s AI infrastructure depends on one company, any significant security or governance problem at Nvidia can create uncertainty across the industry,” Cheung says. Kilcrease echoes those concerns, warning that the scandal could “destabilize” the company. At the very least, she says the various investigations already underway “will consume an immense amount of bandwidth within the company,” creating a very real risk of weighing down Nvidia’s day-to-day operations.

sources.title: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race - New York Post
passages: Beijing’s apparent “honeypot” operation against Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is fresh proof China’s rulers will stop at nothing to win the AI race — yet America’s anti-progress left will surely try to use the scandal to cripple the US industry.

And Huang lobbied Trump to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China, proving “incredibly influential in deciding US export policy for this technology,” frets ex-Secret Service agent Paul Eckloff .

Now that Huang has admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, with surveillance reportedly showing her feeding information to the Chinese (among other alarm bells), the feds absolutely need to probe this case fully, and retaliate accordingly against China.

Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who at first talked about Uncle Sam seizing ownership of half of every AI firm, has switched to pushing legislation aimed at dramatically slowing AI development, with no worries at all that it could let China race ahead.

Yet Huang is the universally recognized driving force of Nvidia, a $4.5 trillion company key to AI development, and some industry sources tell The Post’s Charles Gasparino that he can’t “survive” the blowback his affair has triggered if Democrats use their coming control of Congress to force the issue.

sources.title: Nvidia has a Jensen Huang problem—and no obvious successor
passages: The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company.
“If information was compromised, the implications are a lot bigger than if it was just an affair, which obviously isn’t welcome news,” said a fund manager with a large Nvidia position.
“Nvidia would survive [Huang leaving] but there’s no better person than Jensen to run the company; it would be very different without him.”

Huang’s total compensation last year of $36.3 million, of which the vast majority came in the form of stock awards, included some $4 million for security paid for by Nvidia, which filings say is “due to the exceptionally high public profile and prominence of our CEO.”
The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry.
Huang, who has cultivated an air of infallibility inside Nvidia, has given no indication he will step down from the role of CEO.
Despite his imperial stature, Huang owns just 3.6 percent of Nvidia.
That stake makes him Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder and is worth more than $150 billion.

However, Huang lacks the special voting rights held by many Silicon Valley founders, including Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin, that would allow him to control the board or face down outside investors who might attempt to oust him.

Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter who serves as a senior director in Nvidia’s product marketing team and has become an increasingly visible presence at the company’s conferences, canceled a planned appearance at a company event in South Korea on Monday.
Huang faces a board probe as investors fret over Nvidia’s lack of a clear successor.
“Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post.
These costs included protection at home and during “personal travel,” as well as using private aircraft for all business trips, according to filings.

The board’s public statement on Sunday said it had “confidence in Jensen and his leadership team” and that it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend.
Huang leads a small core executive team at Nvidia, including Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, Operations Chief Debora Shoquist and general counsel Tim Teter.
A 2025 report by law firm Fenwick found that only one company in S&P 100—which would be Nvidia, according to its own filings—had no chair.

Jay Puri, a close lieutenant who led Nvidia’s sales operations and deputized for Huang on international visits, stepped down in August and was replaced on the executive team by Microsoft veteran Nick Parker.

Recent biographies of Huang and Nvidia, including Tae Kim’s The Nvidia Way and Stephen Witt’s The Thinking Machine , portray him as having a rare combination of technical depth and forward-thinking leadership.
In its proxy filings, Nvidia states that this set-up “ensures that each member has an equal voice in the affairs and management of Nvidia.”
The law in Delaware, where Nvidia is incorporated, says executives have certain fiduciary duties including a duty of care and loyalty to their company.
Nvidia’s code of conduct requires executives to “conduct themselves with the highest degree of integrity, ethics and honesty.
Our credibility and reputation depend upon their good judgment, ethical standards and personal integrity.”

extraction.body: Huang faces a board probe as investors fret over Nvidia’s lack of a clear successor. The investigation of Jensen Huang by Nvidia’s board threatens the future of one of Silicon Valley’s longest-serving executives and a key enabler of the AI boom, who has no obvious successor as leader of the world’s second-most-valuable company. Huang is fighting for survival after admitting to an extramarital affair, believed to be with an executive at a large Nvidia customer whom US officials also allege was working as a Chinese spy. The prospect that Huang could be forced out as chief executive of the US chipmaker he co-founded more than 30 years ago has alarmed investors and allies in the tech industry. Shares in Nvidia, which late last month ceded its position as the world’s most valuable to Apple amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks, had fallen more than 5 percent by midday trading on Monday. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” said Shaun Maguire, partner at early Nvidia investor Sequoia Capital, in a social media post. Nvidia’s chips were instrumental in the creation of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and now sit at the center of Big Tech’s $1 trillion AI infrastructure frenzy. Huang has personally stood behind investments and guarantees running into hundreds of billions of dollars for dozens of AI start-ups and data center providers, as well as lobbying US President Donald Trump for looser AI regulation. “Nvidia is not an ordinary company and Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS Nvidia,” analysts at Bernstein said in a note to clients. With policymakers in Washington pressuring Huang to appear before congressional committees to explain himself, the spotlight is on Nvidia’s board, which said on Sunday it would conduct its own “independent” investigation into the scandal that exploded over the weekend. Bill Ackman and Elon Musk are among the powerful business leaders backing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy – as investors hope the longtime exec will be able to survive the scandal. Nvidia – one of the world’s most valuable companies, worth more than $4 trillion – is a largely founder-driven business. Huang has been leading the firm for more than 30 years since he co-founded it and has become synonymous with the AI boom itself. Huang currently has 60 direct reports, no clear successor and a close relationship with President Trump – all of which have stakeholders hoping he’ll remain at the firm, even after he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, an alleged Chinese government spy . Patrick Riccards, a crisis communications expert and former consultant for the Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, told The Post that Nvidia execs are likely hoping to draw out their investigation as long as possible in hopes that the media and public move on to the next scandal. “He’s [Huang] demonstrated his ability to navigate what are very uncertain waters and that has made his board and everybody who owns a piece of this company very, very happy,” Riccards said. “If you get in there and you decide you’re going to replace him … that’s the sort of disruption that could kill a company and nobody wants to see that.” Pershing Square Capital Management CEO Ackman quickly came to Huang’s defense Sunday, after Huang admitted to marital infidelity and wrote an email apologizing to his family and colleagues. “An alert: @JensenHuang is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes. He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward,” Ackman wrote in a post on X Sunday. “I am not suggesting he gets a free pass,” he clarified in a second post. “If indeed this is more than an affair, then it is an [sic] obviously a real problem. I like the guy. He has done a lot of good for the world and I hope the damage here is minimal. That is, I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security.” Musk also replied “I agree” to a post from Shaun Maguire, a venture capitalist and partner at Sequoia, who wrote that while Huang “did something incredibly dumb … my guess is there was no bad intention…and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” President Trump also defended Huang on Sunday, telling reporters that he’s an “honorable guy” and a “fine person,” saying: “He’s done an amazing job for our country.” “I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it,” the president said, adding that he hasn’t yet spoken to the CEO. Dan Ives, tech analyst and partner at Yorkville Ives & Co, said despite the wild scandal, any talk of replacing Huang is “comedy.” Nvidia’s chips are about two to three years ahead of Chinese rivals, he said. “You’re talking about what I would view as the torchbearer – the leader of AI technology – not just in the US but globally,” he told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe.” Dan Gallagher, an analyst at Washington Post Intelligence, argued that Huang has made himself largely indispensable by avoiding traditional bureaucracy – instead maintaining lots of direct reports – and avoiding a designated public successor. “It’s very hard to envision Nvidia run by anybody else,” Gallagher told Axios. “I don’t know if anybody’s going to know how to value Nvidia” without him, he added. Bill Ackman and Elon Musk are among the powerful business leaders backing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy – as investors hope the longtime exec will be able to survive the scandal.

Nvidia – one of the world’s most valuable companies, worth more than $4 trillion – is a largely founder-driven business. Huang has been leading the firm for more than 30 years since he co-founded it and has become synonymous with the AI boom itself.

Huang currently has 60 direct reports, no clear successor and a close relationship with President Trump – all of which have stakeholders hoping he’ll remain at the firm, even after he admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, an alleged Chinese government spy .

Patrick Riccards, a crisis communications expert and former consultant for the Bill Clinton, George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, told The Post that Nvidia execs are likely hoping to draw out their investigation as long as possible in hopes that the media and public move on to the next scandal.

“He’s [Huang] demonstrated his ability to navigate what are very uncertain waters and that has made his board and everybody who owns a piece of this company very, very happy,” Riccards said. “If you get in there and you decide you’re going to replace him … that’s the sort of disruption that could kill a company and nobody wants to see that.”
Pershing Square Capital Management CEO Ackman quickly came to Huang’s defense Sunday, after Huang admitted to marital infidelity and wrote an email apologizing to his family and colleagues.

“An alert: @JensenHuang is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes. He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward,” Ackman wrote in a post on X Sunday.

“I am not suggesting he gets a free pass,” he clarified in a second post. “If indeed this is more than an affair, then it is an [sic] obviously a real problem. I like the guy. He has done a lot of good for the world and I hope the damage here is minimal. That is, I am hoping for a simple affair, not a risk to our national security.”

Musk also replied “I agree” to a post from Shaun Maguire, a venture capitalist and partner at Sequoia, who wrote that while Huang “did something incredibly dumb … my guess is there was no bad intention…and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”
President Trump also defended Huang on Sunday, telling reporters that he’s an “honorable guy” and a “fine person,” saying: “He’s done an amazing job for our country.”
“I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it,” the president said, adding that he hasn’t yet spoken to the CEO.

Dan Ives, tech analyst and partner at Yorkville Ives & Co, said despite the wild scandal, any talk of replacing Huang is “comedy.” Nvidia’s chips are about two to three years ahead of Chinese rivals, he said.
“You’re talking about what I would view as the torchbearer – the leader of AI technology – not just in the US but globally,” he told CNBC’s “Squawk Box Europe.”

Dan Gallagher, an analyst at Washington Post Intelligence, argued that Huang has made himself largely indispensable by avoiding traditional bureaucracy – instead maintaining lots of direct reports – and avoiding a designated public successor.
“It’s very hard to envision Nvidia run by anybody else,” Gallagher told Axios. “I don’t know if anybody’s going to know how to value Nvidia” without him, he added.

Riccards added that Nvidia is almost certainly working with crisis professionals and lawyers, as well as trying to work closely with investigators to make sure their probe of Huang is as narrow as possible.

“It’s going to be really difficult, quite frankly, for any of them to find cold, hard proof that she’s a Chinese spy. It’s not like the Chinese government are going to open up their books,” Riccards said.

Nvidia’s investigation “will confirm that he’s had an affair for X number of years, that he’s had it with this woman, but they won’t be able to confirm any specific role she has played in terms of intelligence community for the Chinese government. I can write you that report right now,” he added.
Huang will also likely try to exude a sense of normalcy by resuming media interviews, meetings with world leaders and public appearances as soon as possible, he predicted.

Huang’s total compensation last year of $36.3 million, of which the vast majority came in the form of stock awards, included some $4 million for security paid for by Nvidia, which filings say is “due to the exceptionally high public profile and prominence of our CEO.”

These costs included protection at home and during “personal travel,” as well as using private aircraft for all business trips, according to filings. Huang reimburses Nvidia for personal air travel on private aircraft arranged by the company, according to filings.

Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . She’s been photographed with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (no relation) at banquet dinners and golf resorts, clinking wine glasses and even leaving an event with him in the same car. However, US officials believe she was also working as a Chinese spy who was having an affair with the Nvidia chief – and tasked with collecting intelligence on one of the world’s most valuable tech giants in an effort to help Beijing surpass the US in AI dominance. The espionage allegations, combined with an admission of an extramarital affair by the Nvidia chief, have rocked the semiconductor behemoth and the broader chip industry. Here’s what we know about the elusive executive in the middle of it all. US Customs and Border Patrol travel records obtained by CNN that correspond with Alice Huang’s social media posts in the US identify her as a 43-year-old Chinese citizen by the name of Huang Le. According to Chinese social media and databases tracking the career of Huang Le, she worked as a journalist for Chinese state television before pivoting to a career in finance. A report from New York Times described Alice Huang as a fluent English speaker who frequented industry conferences and executive dinners, with connections at the highest levels of the AI industry. One Chinese private-equity fund website said Huang had four years of experience in the media and eight in the securities industry, including at HSBC and Citic Securities. From March to November of 2023, Huang was a director at Megaspeed International, according to corporate records in Singapore, where the company is based. The cloud computing and data center provider was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Huang became director and the company changed its name, Megaspeed has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia, purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors by some analyst estimates. Corporate records also indicate Megaspeed received funding from Chinese tech giant Alibaba, and the company has come under investigation for potentially providing Chinese companies with unauthorized access to US chips. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unclear - and she has made no public statement or appearance since last year, when reports of the suspicions surrounding her relationship with Jensen Huang first broke. It is unclear exactly where and when they met, but the Chinese executive has become something of a regular fixture in Huang’s business circles, appearing at the side of the Nvidia CEO at private and corporate events. The two were pictured together as early as September 2024 on WeChat, the ubiquitous Chinese social messaging app, at a luxury golf resort in California. Records from US Customs and Border Protection show Alice Huang has visited the US ten times since 2017. The most recent trip was in March of last year, when she was photographed visiting Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara during the company’s annual conference. Nvidia has previously denied there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about their relationship. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said in statement from October. But on Sunday, the company said it was opening an independent investigation into whether the CEO was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The same weekend Huang admitted to his extramarital affair in a company-wide statement without naming the other party involved. Nvidia, which is worth about $4.5 trillion and designs some of the world’s most advanced AI chips, said as of Sunday that it has no reason to believe that state or corporate secrets had been compromised. The FBI first raised concerns to lawmakers that Alice Huang might be feeding information to China nearly a year ago, two people familiar with the matter told CNN. The New York Times also reported that intelligence officials were conducting electronic surveillance of Alice Huang for at least a year, and had briefed President Donald Trump on the matter last year. Trump said he did not regret not taking action, and downplayed Jensen Huang’s culpability in the incident on Monday. He said he believed that the Nvidia CEO was unaware of any potential motivations of espionage. On Monday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”

extraction.body: Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security. United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.) Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities. As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date. The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum. Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips. Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang. In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported. On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO. “I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said. When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.” Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife. “I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.” “Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote. Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day. Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees. “Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote . “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.” U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship. An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.” U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times. Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo. Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report , U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information. The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump , has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China. Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports. Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service. Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born. These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.” “NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time. extraction.body: Who is Alice Huang, the woman allegedly at the center of the scandal enveloping the world’s most powerful chip company? She’s been photographed with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (no relation) at banquet dinners and golf resorts, clinking wine glasses and even leaving an event with him in the same car. However, US officials believe she was also working as a Chinese spy who was having an affair with the Nvidia chief – and tasked with collecting intelligence on one of the world’s most valuable tech giants in an effort to help Beijing surpass the US in AI dominance. The espionage allegations, combined with an admission of an extramarital affair by the Nvidia chief, have rocked the semiconductor behemoth and the broader chip industry. Here’s what we know about the elusive executive in the middle of it all. US Customs and Border Patrol travel records obtained by CNN that correspond with Alice Huang’s social media posts in the US identify her as a 43-year-old Chinese citizen by the name of Huang Le. According to Chinese social media and databases tracking the career of Huang Le, she worked as a journalist for Chinese state television before pivoting to a career in finance. A report from New York Times described Alice Huang as a fluent English speaker who frequented industry conferences and executive dinners, with connections at the highest levels of the AI industry. One Chinese private-equity fund website said Huang had four years of experience in the media and eight in the securities industry, including at HSBC and Citic Securities. From March to November of 2023, Huang was a director at Megaspeed International, according to corporate records in Singapore, where the company is based. The cloud computing and data center provider was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Huang became director and the company changed its name, Megaspeed has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia, purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors by some analyst estimates. Corporate records also indicate Megaspeed received funding from Chinese tech giant Alibaba, and the company has come under investigation for potentially providing Chinese companies with unauthorized access to US chips. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” Alice Huang’s current whereabouts are unclear - and she has made no public statement or appearance since last year, when reports of the suspicions surrounding her relationship with Jensen Huang first broke. It is unclear exactly where and when they met, but the Chinese executive has become something of a regular fixture in Huang’s business circles, appearing at the side of the Nvidia CEO at private and corporate events. The two were pictured together as early as September 2024 on WeChat, the ubiquitous Chinese social messaging app, at a luxury golf resort in California. Records from US Customs and Border Protection show Alice Huang has visited the US ten times since 2017. The most recent trip was in March of last year, when she was photographed visiting Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara during the company’s annual conference. Nvidia has previously denied there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about their relationship. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the company said in statement from October. But on Sunday, the company said it was opening an independent investigation into whether the CEO was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The same weekend Huang admitted to his extramarital affair in a company-wide statement without naming the other party involved. Nvidia, which is worth about $4.5 trillion and designs some of the world’s most advanced AI chips, said as of Sunday that it has no reason to believe that state or corporate secrets had been compromised. The FBI first raised concerns to lawmakers that Alice Huang might be feeding information to China nearly a year ago, two people familiar with the matter told CNN. The New York Times also reported that intelligence officials were conducting electronic surveillance of Alice Huang for at least a year, and had briefed President Donald Trump on the matter last year. Trump said he did not regret not taking action, and downplayed Jensen Huang’s culpability in the incident on Monday. He said he believed that the Nvidia CEO was unaware of any potential motivations of espionage. On Monday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”

Nvidia makes the processors that power large-scale artificial intelligence systems. U.S. export controls restrict the most advanced of those chips from reaching China, a country competing directly with the United States in AI development. Those rules reflect bipartisan concern that advanced AI processors could accelerate China’s military and surveillance capabilities, which is what transforms the following sequence of events from a corporate personnel matter into a national-security concern.
Jensen Huang leads Nvidia; Alice Huang ran operations at a firm built on Nvidia’s technology.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it since. Alice Huang , also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen and former senior executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-center company that rents computing capacity built on Nvidia processors. She is not related to Jensen Huang.
Media accounts placed the pair together in Taiwan multiple times before any investigation became public.

During 2024 and into 2025 , media reports said Jensen Huang and Alice Huang were photographed or observed socializing in Taiwan, where Jensen Huang was born. Those encounters later became relevant to intelligence reporting about the alleged operation, according to the cited reporting. No public statement about the relationship was identified in that reporting from either Nvidia or U.S. officials at the time.
U.S. and Singapore authorities opened parallel inquiries into whether Nvidia chips reached China through a third-party operator.

In October 2025 , U.S. and Singapore authorities reportedly examined whether Megaspeed had helped Chinese firms, including Alibaba, obtain Nvidia processors in potential violation of U.S. export restrictions. Export controls are rules that restrict the sale of certain advanced technology to designated countries, entities, or uses, sometimes requiring government licensing. Officials also questioned the disposition of Nvidia equipment observed at a Malaysian facility, according to the supplied reporting, as AI is making enforcement of such controls increasingly complex.
The president learned of the intelligence months before it became public.

The New York Times reported that in late 2025, President Trump was informed about intelligence concerning Alice Huang’s alleged activities and her relationship with Jensen Huang. No publicly announced action was identified in the cited reporting at that time. The briefing was not disclosed until reporting on the broader story emerged in late October 2026.
U.S. officials reportedly concluded Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, though that assessment has not been independently verified.

In spring 2026 , U.S. officials reportedly circulated a classified memo alleging that Alice Huang was an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security , the country’s primary civilian intelligence agency. The memo allegedly stated she had been recruited to gather information about Jensen Huang . It also alleged she was tasked with influencing Nvidia’s commercial position on advanced chip sales to China. This is an intelligence assessment reported by news organizations citing unnamed officials; it is not an established legal or investigative finding. Such government restrictions on technology access echo broader debates over how authorities worldwide handle sensitive data, as seen when Europe restricts major cloud providers from handling sensitive public-sector information.
A New York Times report in October 2026 brought the relationship and the investigation into public view.

On October 29, 2026 , the New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year and that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Nvidia responded by characterizing Jensen Huang’s interactions with her as ordinary customer-related contact. A rapid sequence of corporate and political responses followed that disclosure.
Three House committee chairmen asked Jensen Huang to appear before a closed-door session.

The chairmen of the House Select Committee on China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and the House Intelligence Committee formally requested a closed-door briefing from Jensen Huang, with the request reported around November 5, 2026. The letter cited concerns about Chinese access to sensitive U.S. technology and possible infiltration of American technology companies. No public response from Huang or Nvidia was identified in the cited reporting at that time.
The CEO issued a public apology on November 8 without naming Alice Huang.

On November 8, 2026 , Jensen Huang publicly acknowledged that he had been unfaithful, apologizing to his wife, children, Nvidia employees, and the company. He linked his statement to national-security concerns described in media coverage but did not identify Alice Huang by name. He also withdrew from planned appearances at the ElevenLabs Summit and the Anthropic CEO Forum.
The board acted the following day, saying it had no immediate evidence of compromised secrets.

On November 9, 2026 , Nvidia’s board announced an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason at that stage to believe Nvidia secrets or U.S. national security had been compromised. President Trump said Jensen Huang should remain CEO. Trump later added that Huang had told him he did not know Alice Huang was allegedly a spy.
Beijing’s Foreign Ministry called the espionage claim “groundless speculation.”

On November 10, 2026 , China’s Foreign Ministry characterized the allegation that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence as a smear and rejected it as unsubstantiated. Corporate records, as reported by media, separately identified her as a Megaspeed director from March to November 2023. The supplied reporting does not identify her current status or whereabouts.
The investigation is ongoing, and several core questions have no public answers yet.

Public reporting has not established what information Alice Huang allegedly obtained, whether any Nvidia proprietary information was transferred, or whether export-control violations involving Megaspeed occurred. Nvidia’s independent board investigation has not released findings. Congressional committees have requested access to Jensen Huang ; no hearing date has been announced, and until investigators publish conclusions or authorities bring formal charges, the espionage allegations remain unproven.

extraction.body: Envoy Medical Inc. (NASDAQ: COCH ) on Tuesday said it surpassed the three-month milestone for all 56 patients enrolled in the company's pivotal clinical trial evaluating the investigational fully implanted Acclaim cochlear implant. The update marks another important clinical trial milestone as the company continues to build momentum with the hearing industry . Read Also: EXCLUSIVE: Envoy Medical Hits Trial Milestone For Cochlear Implant Designed To Work With Natural Ear "Envoy Medical continues to demonstrate its ability to execute," said Brent Lucas , CEO of Envoy Medical. "Each milestone achieved brings us one big step closer to our next major goal – submission of our PMA application to the FDA." The company is continuing to collect safety and other study measures as part of its ongoing pivotal trial, with full data to be included as part of its planned Premarket Approval (PMA) submission to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Envoy Medical anticipates achieving its six-month visit milestone by late 2026 and its 12-month visit milestone for the entire study by April 2027. Acclaim Cochlear Implant is an investigational hearing device. Envoy Medical's fully implanted technology includes a sensor designed to leverage the natural anatomy of the ear instead of a microphone to capture sound. The Acclaim implant is designed to address severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss that is not adequately addressed by hearing aids. Last week, Envoy Medical reported 12-month results from the first 10 participants in Stage 1 of its pivotal clinical trial evaluating the investigational fully implanted Acclaim cochlear implant, with hearing performance continuing to improve over previously reported six-month data. The company said participants achieved a mean Consonant-Nucleus-Consonant word recognition score of 53.2% at the 12-month mark, compared with a pre-implantation baseline of 15.2%. The 38.0 percentage point improvement exceeded the 24.0 percentage point gain reported after six months, when the cohort posted a mean score of 39.2%. COCH Price Action: Envoy Medical shares were up 1.34% at $0.68 during premarket trading on Tuesday, according to Benzinga Pro data . Newswise — CLEVELAND – University Hospitals is bringing the next generation of hearing technology to patients in Northeast Ohio as the only site in the state participating in a Phase 3 clinical trial evaluating the Totally Implantable Cochlear Implant (TICI). The ELEVATE trial is studying this investigational device which is designed to provide hearing without any external components. Unlike conventional cochlear implants which include both an implanted component and an external sound processor worn behind the ear, the investigational TICI system is designed for placement completely under the skin. The microphone and battery are implanted, allowing users to hear without any visible external device. “We’re excited to see any potential benefits,” said Alejandro Rivas, MD, Division Chief of Otology and Neurotology, and Director of the Cochlear Implant Program at University Hospitals, as well as the Principal Investigator for the ELEVATE trial at UH. “Today, most patients with cochlear implants remove the outer component when they sleep, shower, and if they go swimming. This means they’re totally deaf at those times, which is an inconvenience and also a safety hazard.” The concept of a TICI has been pursued for decades but has faced significant engineering challenges. One of the biggest obstacles is managing sounds generated by the body itself, including muscle movement, swallowing, and other internal noises that an implanted microphone can detect. Advances in technology and sophisticated algorithms have created a pathway for large-scale clinical evaluation. Three patients recently received the TICI device at University Hospitals, filling the institution’s allocated enrollment slots in the trial. Participants are adults with moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss and poor speech understanding. They will be followed for one year to evaluate hearing performance and safety. The study is sponsored by Cochlear, a global leader in implantable hearing solutions. Trial enrollment is now concluded for 56 participants at 11 national sites. University Hospitals was selected to participate in the trial based on its past experience in cochlear implant research. The experienced site team at UH includes co-investigator Cameron Wick, MD, otologist/neurotologist, and audiologist Viral Tejani, AuD, PhD. “Participation in studies like this demonstrates UH’s commitment to innovation,” said Nicole Maronian, MD, Chair of the Department of Otolaryngology – Head and Neck Surgery, and the Director of the UH Ear Nose and Throat Institute. “Our patients don’t have to travel outside the region to access cutting-edge therapies. We’re able to bring this potentially groundbreaking technology directly to Northeast Ohio while helping shape the future of hearing restoration.” Investigators also hope the technology may eventually encourage more people to consider cochlear implantation. Despite evidence showing the benefits of cochlear implants for many individuals with significant hearing loss, less than 5 percent of eligible adults currently receive one. “A large number of people who could benefit from cochlear implants choose not to pursue them,” said Dr. Rivas, who is also the Richard W. and Patricia R. Pogue Chair in Auditory Surgery and Hearing Sciences. “For some, concerns about wearing an external device are part of the decision. If fully implantable technology proves successful, it may help expand access to hearing restoration for patients who have been reluctant to consider cochlear implantation.” No totally implantable cochlear implant is currently commercially available in the United States. The ELEVATE trial is an important step in evaluating the safety and effectiveness of this investigational system. As the only Ohio institution participating in the study, University Hospitals continues its mission of delivering leading-edge care, giving patients access to innovative technologies that have the potential to redefine treatment options and improve quality of life. Consultancy Disclosure: Alejandro Rivas, Cameron Wick, and Viral Tejani have provided independent consulting services to Cochlear within the past 12 months. The main campus also includes the UH Rainbow Babies & Children's Hospital, ranked among the top children’s hospitals in the nation; UH MacDonald Women's Hospital, Ohio's only hospital for women; and UH Seidman Cancer Center, part of the NCI-designated Case Comprehensive Cancer Center. UH is home to some of the most prestigious clinical and research programs in the nation, with more than 3,000 active clinical trials and research studies underway. Unlike conventional cochlear implants which include both an implanted component and an external sound processor worn behind the ear, the investigational TICI system is designed for placement completely under the skin. The microphone and battery are implanted, allowing users to hear without any visible external device.

“We’re excited to see any potential benefits,” said Alejandro Rivas, MD, Division Chief of Otology and Neurotology, and Director of the Cochlear Implant Program at University Hospitals, as well as the Principal Investigator for the ELEVATE trial at UH. “Today, most patients with cochlear implants remove the outer component when they sleep, shower, and if they go swimming. This means they’re totally deaf at those times, which is an inconvenience and also a safety hazard.”

The concept of a TICI has been pursued for decades but has faced significant engineering challenges. One of the biggest obstacles is managing sounds generated by the body itself, including muscle movement, swallowing, and other internal noises that an implanted microphone can detect. Advances in technology and sophisticated algorithms have created a pathway for large-scale clinical evaluation.

Three patients recently received the TICI device at University Hospitals, filling the institution’s allocated enrollment slots in the trial. Participants are adults with moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss and poor speech understanding. They will be followed for one year to evaluate hearing performance and safety. The study is sponsored by Cochlear, a global leader in implantable hearing solutions. Trial enrollment is now concluded for 56 participants at 11 national sites.

University Hospitals was selected to participate in the trial based on its past experience in cochlear implant research. The experienced site team at UH includes co-investigator Cameron Wick, MD, otologist/neurotologist, and audiologist Viral Tejani, AuD, PhD.

“Participation in studies like this demonstrates UH’s commitment to innovation,” said Nicole Maronian, MD, Chair of the Department of Otolaryngology – Head and Neck Surgery, and the Director of the UH Ear Nose and Throat Institute. “Our patients don’t have to travel outside the region to access cutting-edge therapies. Investigators also hope the technology may eventually encourage more people to consider cochlear implantation. Despite evidence showing the benefits of cochlear implants for many individuals with significant hearing loss, less than 5 percent of eligible adults currently receive one.

“A large number of people who could benefit from cochlear implants choose not to pursue them,” said Dr. Rivas, who is also the Richard W. and Patricia R. Pogue Chair in Auditory Surgery and Hearing Sciences. “For some, concerns about wearing an external device are part of the decision. If fully implantable technology proves successful, it may help expand access to hearing restoration for patients who have been reluctant to consider cochlear implantation.”

No totally implantable cochlear implant is currently commercially available in the United States. The ELEVATE trial is an important step in evaluating the safety and effectiveness of this investigational system.

As the only Ohio institution participating in the study, University Hospitals continues its mission of delivering leading-edge care, giving patients access to innovative technologies that have the potential to redefine treatment options and improve quality of life.
