Newswise — CLEVELAND – University Hospitals is bringing the next generation of hearing technology to patients in Northeast Ohio as the only site in the state participating in a Phase 3 clinical trial evaluating the Totally Implantable Cochlear Implant (TICI). The ELEVATE trial is studying this investigational device which is designed to provide hearing without any external components. Unlike conventional cochlear implants which include both an implanted component and an external sound processor worn behind the ear, the investigational TICI system is designed for placement completely under the skin. The microphone and battery are implanted, allowing users to hear without any visible external device. “We’re excited to see any potential benefits,” said Alejandro Rivas, MD, Division Chief of Otology and Neurotology, and Director of the Cochlear Implant Program at University Hospitals, as well as the Principal Investigator for the ELEVATE trial at UH. “Today, most patients with cochlear implants remove the outer component when they sleep, shower, and if they go swimming. This means they’re totally deaf at those times, which is an inconvenience and also a safety hazard.” The concept of a TICI has been pursued for decades but has faced significant engineering challenges. One of the biggest obstacles is managing sounds generated by the body itself, including muscle movement, swallowing, and other internal noises that an implanted microphone can detect. Advances in technology and sophisticated algorithms have created a pathway for large-scale clinical evaluation. Three patients recently received the TICI device at University Hospitals, filling the institution’s allocated enrollment slots in the trial. Participants are adults with moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss and poor speech understanding. They will be followed for one year to evaluate hearing performance and safety. The study is sponsored by Cochlear, a global leader in implantable hearing solutions. Trial enrollment is now concluded for 56 participants at 11 national sites. University Hospitals was selected to participate in the trial based on its past experience in cochlear implant research. The experienced site team at UH includes co-investigator Cameron Wick, MD, otologist/neurotologist, and audiologist Viral Tejani, AuD, PhD. “Participation in studies like this demonstrates UH’s commitment to innovation,” said Nicole Maronian, MD, Chair of the Department of Otolaryngology – Head and Neck Surgery, and the Director of the UH Ear Nose and Throat Institute. “Our patients don’t have to travel outside the region to access cutting-edge therapies. We’re able to bring this potentially groundbreaking technology directly to Northeast Ohio while helping shape the future of hearing restoration.” Investigators also hope the technology may eventually encourage more people to consider cochlear implantation. Despite evidence showing the benefits of cochlear implants for many individuals with significant hearing loss, less than 5 percent of eligible adults currently receive one. “A large number of people who could benefit from cochlear implants choose not to pursue them,” said Dr. Rivas, who is also the Richard W. and Patricia R. Pogue Chair in Auditory Surgery and Hearing Sciences. “For some, concerns about wearing an external device are part of the decision. If fully implantable technology proves successful, it may help expand access to hearing restoration for patients who have been reluctant to consider cochlear implantation.” No totally implantable cochlear implant is currently commercially available in the United States. The ELEVATE trial is an important step in evaluating the safety and effectiveness of this investigational system. As the only Ohio institution participating in the study, University Hospitals continues its mission of delivering leading-edge care, giving patients access to innovative technologies that have the potential to redefine treatment options and improve quality of life. Consultancy Disclosure: Alejandro Rivas, Cameron Wick, and Viral Tejani have provided independent consulting services to Cochlear within the past 12 months. The system’s flagship quaternary care, academic medical center, University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, is affiliated with Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine, Northeast Ohio Medical University, Oxford University, the Technion Israel Institute of Technology and National Taiwan University College of Medicine. The main campus also includes the UH Rainbow Babies & Children's Hospital, ranked among the top children’s hospitals in the nation; UH MacDonald Women's Hospital, Ohio's only hospital for women; and UH Seidman Cancer Center, part of the NCI-designated Case Comprehensive Cancer Center. UH is home to some of the most prestigious clinical and research programs in the nation, with more than 3,000 active clinical trials and research studies underway. UH Cleveland Medical Center is perennially among the highest performers in national ranking surveys, including “America’s Best Hospitals” from U.S. News & World Report. UH is also home to 19 Clinical Care Delivery and Research Institutes. UH is one of the largest employers in Northeast Ohio with more than 30,000 employees. University Hospitals was selected to participate in the trial based on its past experience in cochlear implant research. The experienced site team at UH includes co-investigator Cameron Wick, MD, otologist/neurotologist, and audiologist Viral Tejani, AuD, PhD.

“Participation in studies like this demonstrates UH’s commitment to innovation,” said Nicole Maronian, MD, Chair of the Department of Otolaryngology – Head and Neck Surgery, and the Director of the UH Ear Nose and Throat Institute. “Our patients don’t have to travel outside the region to access cutting-edge therapies. We’re able to bring this potentially groundbreaking technology directly to Northeast Ohio while helping shape the future of hearing restoration.”

Investigators also hope the technology may eventually encourage more people to consider cochlear implantation. Despite evidence showing the benefits of cochlear implants for many individuals with significant hearing loss, less than 5 percent of eligible adults currently receive one.

“A large number of people who could benefit from cochlear implants choose not to pursue them,” said Dr. Rivas, who is also the Richard W. and Patricia R. Pogue Chair in Auditory Surgery and Hearing Sciences. “For some, concerns about wearing an external device are part of the decision. If fully implantable technology proves successful, it may help expand access to hearing restoration for patients who have been reluctant to consider cochlear implantation.”

No totally implantable cochlear implant is currently commercially available in the United States. The ELEVATE trial is an important step in evaluating the safety and effectiveness of this investigational system.

As the only Ohio institution participating in the study, University Hospitals continues its mission of delivering leading-edge care, giving patients access to innovative technologies that have the potential to redefine treatment options and improve quality of life.

Envoy Medical Inc. has completed clinical trial enrollment for the investigational fully implanted Acclaim cochlear implant. With the 56th and final patient having received the device, the company reports that it has become the first cochlear implant manufacturer to complete full U.S. clinical trial enrollment for evaluating a fully implanted cochlear implant system. “Completing enrollment of a pivotal clinical trial that is evaluating a breakthrough-designated medical device that has the potential to bring about generational change to an entire industry is a very big deal,” Envoy Medical CEO Brent Lucas said. “We strongly believe in our device design and look forward to gathering additional data throughout the trial as we substantially differentiate ourselves from the competition. We believe today brings us significantly closer to redefining the standard of care for adults with severe to profound hearing loss and potentially growing the overall cochlear implant user base to include those patients who could benefit from a cochlear implant but have sat on the sidelines waiting for a fully implanted solution.” The final two study participants were both implanted yesterday (March 10) by Dr. Patrick Antonelli at the University of Florida. With these procedures, Dr. Antonelli became the second leading enroller in the trial, having implanted 11 of the 56 participants. “Participating in the Acclaim Cochlear Implant Pivotal Trial has been an eye opener for me,” Dr. Antonelli shared. “I’ve been placing traditional cochlear implants for so long—over 30 years—and these devices evolved so little over that time that I didn’t give much thought to how dramatically they could be improved. The Acclaim changed that. People with profound hearing loss desperately want to be able to hear 24/7 without having to wear an external processor. Others have been reluctant to get a cochlear implant because of the stigma they feel with an external processor. I think just about every Acclaim recipient that we’ve enrolled in this study said, often tearfully, ‘You’ve really made my day,’ when I told them they were cleared to get the Acclaim. I am delighted that completion of study enrollment brings us a step closer to FDA approval and hopefully being able to offer the Acclaim to all of our properly qualified patients.” With enrollment completed, the study will now progress through scheduled follow-up visits and data collection in accordance with trial protocol. The product addresses severe to profound sensorineural hearing loss that is not adequately addressed by current hearing aid solutions. The Esteem fully implanted active middle ear implant (FI-AMEI) is the only FDA-approved, fully implanted* hearing device for adults diagnosed with moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss allowing for 24/7 hearing capability using the ear’s natural anatomy. sources.title: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
passages: Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million.
The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating.
By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians.
Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release .
Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV.
PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.

“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care.
From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.
Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30.

extraction.body: Oura just made its biggest bet yet on AI-powered healthcare, announcing a $625 million acquisition of Counsel Health, an AI-native primary care startup. The deal comes just weeks after the smart ring maker postponed its $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing market uncertainty. The move signals a major strategic shift for Oura - from hardware maker to integrated health services platform - and represents one of the largest healthtech acquisitions of 2026. The Finnish smart ring maker announced today it's acquiring Counsel Health, an AI-native primary care startup, for $625 million in a mix of cash and stock. It's a bold move that transforms Oura from a hardware company into something much bigger - a vertically integrated health platform that combines biometric tracking with actual medical care. Just weeks ago, Oura postponed its planned IPO that could have valued the company at up to $2.2 billion. The company cited "uncertainty in the IPO market" as the reason for the delay. Now, instead of going public, Oura is doubling down on a strategy that could redefine what a wearables company can be. Counsel Health brings AI-powered primary care directly to patients, using machine learning models to triage symptoms, recommend treatments, and connect users with human physicians when needed. The startup's technology analyzes patient data in real-time, offering personalized health guidance that goes far beyond what a fitness tracker can provide. For Oura, which has built its reputation on sleep and recovery tracking through its signature ring, the acquisition opens a direct path to monetizing the health data it collects. The deal puts Oura in direct competition with tech giants circling the healthcare space. Apple has been steadily adding health features to the Apple Watch, while Amazon continues to expand its pharmacy and telehealth services. But Oura's approach is different - it's betting that combining passive biometric monitoring with AI-driven care can create a seamless health experience that neither pure hardware nor pure software companies can match. The $625 million price tag is significant, especially for a company that just pulled its IPO. It suggests Oura either has strong backing from existing investors or is confident enough in its cash position to make this bet. The company has raised over $300 million from investors including Dexcom, Eisai, and several high-profile individuals. Those backers are now betting on a very different company than the one they initially funded. This acquisition fits into a broader pattern of AI tools driving up healthcare costs, with Blue Cross Blue Shield data showing AI adoption led to nearly $1 billion in additional spending over two years. But Oura is betting it can flip that equation - using AI to make primary care more efficient and accessible, not more expensive. Even Healthcare recently hit a $300M valuation with backing from Khosla Ventures, while countless startups are racing to apply AI to everything from diagnostics to drug discovery. Counsel Health's acquisition suggests the consolidation phase is beginning, with established players like Oura buying technology rather than building it from scratch. For Oura's existing users, the acquisition could mean their sleep and activity data suddenly becomes far more actionable. The execution will depend on how well Oura can integrate Counsel Health's technology with its hardware and whether users are comfortable with that level of data sharing. The deal also raises questions about Oura's path to profitability. The company has been burning cash to grow its user base and develop new products. Adding a primary care service could create a recurring revenue stream through subscription fees or insurance partnerships, but it also adds complexity and regulatory burden. Healthcare is a notoriously difficult business, with thin margins and heavy compliance requirements. Oura's pivot mirrors moves by other wearables companies struggling to differentiate in a crowded market. Fitbit sold to Google for $2.1 billion in 2021. Whoop remains private but has raised hundreds of millions to build out its subscription model. The hardware alone isn't enough anymore - companies need services, data insights, and deeper integration into users' lives to justify their valuations. The acquisition comes at a time when privacy concerns are mounting around AI wearables, with regulators and consumers increasingly wary of how health data gets used. Oura will need to navigate those concerns carefully as it integrates Counsel Health's AI capabilities. Counsel Health's team and technology will be integrated into Oura's operations, though details on timing and how the service will be offered remain unclear. Will it be bundled with Oura's existing subscription?

While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating.
By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians.
Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.

“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release .

It's a bold move that transforms Oura from a hardware company into something much bigger - a vertically integrated health platform that combines biometric tracking with actual medical care. Just weeks ago, Oura postponed its planned IPO that could have valued the company at up to $2.2 billion. The company cited "uncertainty in the IPO market" as the reason for the delay. Now, instead of going public, Oura is doubling down on a strategy that could redefine what a wearables company can be. Counsel Health brings AI-powered primary care directly to patients, using machine learning models to triage symptoms, recommend treatments, and connect users with human physicians when needed. The startup's technology analyzes patient data in real-time, offering personalized health guidance that goes far beyond what a fitness tracker can provide. For Oura, which has built its reputation on sleep and recovery tracking through its signature ring, the acquisition opens a direct path to monetizing the health data it collects. The deal puts Oura in direct competition with tech giants circling the healthcare space. Apple has been steadily adding health features to the Apple Watch, while Amazon continues to expand its pharmacy and telehealth services. But Oura's approach is different - it's betting that combining passive biometric monitoring with AI-driven care can create a seamless health experience that neither pure hardware nor pure software companies can match. The $625 million price tag is significant, especially for a company that just pulled its IPO. It suggests Oura either has strong backing from existing investors or is confident enough in its cash position to make this bet. The company has raised over $300 million from investors including Dexcom, Eisai, and several high-profile individuals. Those backers are now betting on a very different company than the one they initially funded. This acquisition fits into a broader pattern of AI tools driving up healthcare costs, with Blue Cross Blue Shield data showing AI adoption led to nearly $1 billion in additional spending over two years. But Oura is betting it can flip that equation - using AI to make primary care more efficient and accessible, not more expensive. Even Healthcare recently hit a $300M valuation with backing from Khosla Ventures, while countless startups are racing to apply AI to everything from diagnostics to drug discovery. Counsel Health's acquisition suggests the consolidation phase is beginning, with established players like Oura buying technology rather than building it from scratch. For Oura's existing users, the acquisition could mean their sleep and activity data suddenly becomes far more actionable. The execution will depend on how well Oura can integrate Counsel Health's technology with its hardware and whether users are comfortable with that level of data sharing. The deal also raises questions about Oura's path to profitability. The company has been burning cash to grow its user base and develop new products. Adding a primary care service could create a recurring revenue stream through subscription fees or insurance partnerships, but it also adds complexity and regulatory burden. Healthcare is a notoriously difficult business, with thin margins and heavy compliance requirements. Oura's pivot mirrors moves by other wearables companies struggling to differentiate in a crowded market. Fitbit sold to Google for $2.1 billion in 2021. Whoop remains private but has raised hundreds of millions to build out its subscription model. The hardware alone isn't enough anymore - companies need services, data insights, and deeper integration into users' lives to justify their valuations. The acquisition comes at a time when privacy concerns are mounting around AI wearables, with regulators and consumers increasingly wary of how health data gets used. Oura will need to navigate those concerns carefully as it integrates Counsel Health's AI capabilities. Counsel Health's team and technology will be integrated into Oura's operations, though details on timing and how the service will be offered remain unclear. Will it be bundled with Oura's existing subscription?

passages: Disney is bringing more than 60 3D movies to the Disney Plus app on Meta Quest.
The 3D movies you can check out include The Avengers and Black Panther, Meta says.

extraction.body: Disney is bringing more than 60 3D movies to the Disney Plus app on Meta Quest. The movies will be available to Disney Plus subscribers as part of an updated Disney Plus app that’s rolling out today. The 3D movies you can check out include The Avengers and Black Panther, Meta says. But the updated Quest app doesn’t just offer 3D movies; you’ll also be able to see some films in themed, immersive virtual environments, like a Tatooine environment when watching Star Wars: A New Hope or a Scare Floor one for Monsters, Inc. I got to see an Avengers-themed immersive environment for myself while trying Meta’s forthcoming VR Glasses in September, and while it was novel for the few minutes I tried it, I wasn’t sure if it would be good during an entire movie. The Disney Plus app on the VR Glasses, which are set to release sometime in spring 2027, will also let you watch IMAX Enhanced movies, including Avengers: Endgame, Lightyear, and Tron: Ares. The VR Glasses will also be a place to watch 3D movies from Lionsgate.

sources.title: Be Transported Into Your Favorite Disney+ Stories with 3D Movies and Immersive Environments On Meta Quest and Meta VR Glasses - www.meta.com
passages: Your favorite movies and TV shows are now more immersive than ever on Meta VR devices.

As we announced at Connect 2026 , we’ve joined forces with Disney to upgrade the Disney+ app on Meta Quest with 3D content*, and starting today, subscribers can stream more than 60 movies like Marvel’s The Avengers and Marvel Studios’ Black Panther, and more in 3D in select countries.
You can look forward to an even broader selection of great content and unparalleled viewing when Meta VR Glasses launch in spring 2027.
The glasses’ 5K Infinite Display, built on micro-OLED panels, allows us to create an incredible-looking picture, giving you a personal theater wherever you are.
And Disney+ doesn’t just offer 3D movies — it’s also bringing you IMAX Enhanced movies such as Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Endgame, Disney and Pixar’s Lightyear , Tron: Ares , and a whole lot more.
The upgraded Disney+ turns movie watching into an experience, thanks to immersive themed environments that surround you while you watch.

The upgraded Disney+ is available right now on the Meta Horizon Store .

Three posters on a leaked screen do not answer that.

extraction.body: A limited selection of 3D movies has begun appearing in the TV app on Quest headsets, and datamining suggests that 3D movies may become a benefit of the Meta Horizon+ subscription service. At Meta Connect 2026 in September, alongside the reveal of Meta VR Glasses , the company announced that Quest owners in the US would be able to rent or buy "hundreds" of movies in late 2026. The company said that this catalog will eventually expand to "thousands" of titles available internationally by the time Meta VR Glasses launch in 2027. Now, some Quest 3 and 3S owners have spotted a limited selection of 3D movies in the TV app, while Meta has also added new support articles describing the ability to rent or buy media. The movies listed so far appear to consist primarily of Disney-owned content. Notably, they can be purchased directly through the Meta Horizon Store without an active Disney+ subscription. Separately, the Disney+ app is set to receive its own overhaul on the platform this month, bringing a new spatial UI, support for 3D media, and several of the immersive environments also available in the Disney+ app for visionOS on Apple Vision Pro. Additionally, a page discovered in the TV app by user Nikita and shared by dataminer and programmer Nori suggests that Meta may begin offering 3D movies as part of the Horizon+ subscription service. The page also suggests that the service may be rebranded as Meta VR+. Such a rebrand would fit with the company's broader efforts to separate Horizon Worlds and related branding from the Quest platform, which began earlier this year . If you're unfamiliar, Meta Horizon+ is the company's $8/month (or $60/year) subscription service for its VR devices. Subscribers get access to a Games Catalog of around 50 major VR titles, as well as an Indie Catalog of around 50 smaller titles, for a total of around 100 games. In February 2026, Meta reported that the subscription service had crossed 1 million "active subscribers" in 2025 . In July, the company also added a starter edition of Xbox Game Pass to Horizon+, giving subscribers access to 50+ games and 10 hours of cloud gaming each month. More recently, the service has started regularly offering subscribers exclusive game discounts and free add-ons for games. Adding 3D movies to Horizon+ would align with the media focus of Meta VR Glasses and recent Horizon OS updates , as well as the strategy outlined by Meta Director of Games Chris Pruett at GDC in March. Pruett stated that the company expects "more Mainstream Adults to enter VR through media consumption first, then discover games once they are in-headset" over the next couple of years. coreStoryFacts.text: Disney is bringing more than 60 3D movies to the Disney Plus app on Meta Quest.
The 3D movies you can check out include The Avengers and Black Panther, Meta says.

I got to see an Avengers-themed immersive environment for myself while trying Meta’s forthcoming VR Glasses in September, and while it was novel for the few minutes I tried it, I wasn’t sure if it would be good during an entire movie.
Your favorite movies and TV shows are now more immersive than ever on Meta VR devices.

As we announced at Connect 2026 , we’ve joined forces with Disney to upgrade the Disney+ app on Meta Quest with 3D content*, and starting today, subscribers can stream more than 60 movies like Marvel’s The Avengers and Marvel Studios’ Black Panther, and more in 3D in select countries.
You can look forward to an even broader selection of great content and unparalleled viewing when Meta VR Glasses launch in spring 2027.
The glasses’ 5K Infinite Display, built on micro-OLED panels, allows us to create an incredible-looking picture, giving you a personal theater wherever you are.
And Disney+ doesn’t just offer 3D movies — it’s also bringing you IMAX Enhanced movies such as Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Endgame, Disney and Pixar’s Lightyear , Tron: Ares , and a whole lot more.
The upgraded Disney+ turns movie watching into an experience, thanks to immersive themed environments that surround you while you watch.
The screen carries one heading: "3D Movies included in your subscription." Beneath it, in smaller grey type, sits a subscription name Meta has never used in public.
The leak lands on top of a movie plan Meta laid out at Connect, covered here on September 23 .

Meta's blog said "you'll be able to rent or buy hundreds of movies later this year on Meta Quest in the US." The newsroom post promised "new 3D movies releasing every month," an IMAX Enhanced certification for the glasses and "first time in 3D" releases with James Cameron's Lightstorm Vision in 2027.
Three posters on a leaked screen do not answer that.
A Sony film inside a Meta subscription would still be a deal nobody has announced.
The screen spells out "Meta VR Plus." The post that shared it says "Meta VR+."
Meta renamed Quest+ to Horizon+ on May 7, 2025 , in a post headed "New Name, Same Great Subscription," and gave no reason.
Meta VR is also the name on the $1,299.99 Meta VR Glasses , which Meta says ship in spring 2027 and which do not carry the Quest name.
Those are the same two numbers Meta put on it when the service launched as Quest+ on June 26, 2023 .

As we announced at Connect 2026 , we’ve joined forces with Disney to upgrade the Disney+ app on Meta Quest with 3D content*, and starting today, subscribers can stream more than 60 movies like Marvel’s The Avengers and Marvel Studios’ Black Panther, and more in 3D in select countries. Disney+ now includes a host of content options in 3D on Meta VR devices, so you’re not just seeing a great movie on a big, personal screen; you’re getting another dimension — complete with Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision*. See heroes leap off the screen and get absorbed into your favorite stories like never before. The upgraded Disney+ turns movie watching into an experience, thanks to immersive themed environments that surround you while you watch. Catch Star Wars: A New Hope (Episode IV) from a comfy spot on Tatooine, see the Avengers battle Loki from atop Avengers Tower, settle in for a Pixar movie night on the Monsters, Inc. Scare Floor, and more. Each of the environments is full of evocative details that will make you feel like you’ve been transported while you watch. You can look forward to an even broader selection of great content and unparalleled viewing when Meta VR Glasses launch in spring 2027. The glasses’ 5K Infinite Display, built on micro-OLED panels, allows us to create an incredible-looking picture, giving you a personal theater wherever you are. And Disney+ doesn’t just offer 3D movies — it’s also bringing you IMAX Enhanced movies such as Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Endgame, Disney and Pixar’s Lightyear , Tron: Ares , and a whole lot more. Best of all, these new moviegoing experiences from Disney are included in your subscription, alongside all the 2D content you already know and love. The upgraded Disney+ is available right now on the Meta Horizon Store .

Disney+ now includes a host of content options in 3D on Meta VR devices, so you’re not just seeing a great movie on a big, personal screen; you’re getting another dimension — complete with Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision*. See heroes leap off the screen and get absorbed into your favorite stories like never before.

The upgraded Disney+ turns movie watching into an experience, thanks to immersive themed environments that surround you while you watch. Catch Star Wars: A New Hope (Episode IV) from a comfy spot on Tatooine, see the Avengers battle Loki from atop Avengers Tower, settle in for a Pixar movie night on the Monsters, Inc. Scare Floor, and more. Each of the environments is full of evocative details that will make you feel like you’ve been transported while you watch.

You can look forward to an even broader selection of great content and unparalleled viewing when Meta VR Glasses launch in spring 2027. The glasses’ 5K Infinite Display, built on micro-OLED panels, allows us to create an incredible-looking picture, giving you a personal theater wherever you are. And Disney+ doesn’t just offer 3D movies — it’s also bringing you IMAX Enhanced movies such as Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Endgame, Disney and Pixar’s Lightyear , Tron: Ares , and a whole lot more.

Best of all, these new moviegoing experiences from Disney are included in your subscription, alongside all the 2D content you already know and love. The upgraded Disney+ is available right now on the Meta Horizon Store .

Three posters fill the row: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Project Hail Mary and Spider-Man: Far From Home. Below them are channel tiles for Disney+, MLB and Prime Video. The dataminer Nori posted the capture on X on Sunday and credited the find to another user, NT2182. The post hedges twice: "Meta may be planning to rebrand 'Horizon+' as 'Meta VR+' and they may include monthly movies as part of the benefits!" 9to5Google picked it up on Monday. Meta has not commented. The screen shows no price, no date and no country. Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 is a 2023 Marvel Studios film released by Disney. It also includes a starter edition of Xbox Game Pass capped at 10 hours of cloud play a month, which Evan read in July as a hallway to the full Game Pass . Horizon+ still costs what it cost in 2023, and Meta has announced no new tier. For a current subscriber, films would be an addition, unless the rename arrives with a new price. Anyone paying monthly already spends $35.89 a year more than the annual plan for the option to cancel. extraction.body: A limited selection of 3D movies has begun appearing in the TV app on Quest headsets, and datamining suggests that 3D movies may become a benefit of the Meta Horizon+ subscription service. At Meta Connect 2026 in September, alongside the reveal of Meta VR Glasses , the company announced that Quest owners in the US would be able to rent or buy "hundreds" of movies in late 2026. The company said that this catalog will eventually expand to "thousands" of titles available internationally by the time Meta VR Glasses launch in 2027. Now, some Quest 3 and 3S owners have spotted a limited selection of 3D movies in the TV app, while Meta has also added new support articles describing the ability to rent or buy media. The movies listed so far appear to consist primarily of Disney-owned content. Notably, they can be purchased directly through the Meta Horizon Store without an active Disney+ subscription. Separately, the Disney+ app is set to receive its own overhaul on the platform this month, bringing a new spatial UI, support for 3D media, and several of the immersive environments also available in the Disney+ app for visionOS on Apple Vision Pro. Additionally, a page discovered in the TV app by user Nikita and shared by dataminer and programmer Nori suggests that Meta may begin offering 3D movies as part of the Horizon+ subscription service. The page also suggests that the service may be rebranded as Meta VR+. Such a rebrand would fit with the company's broader efforts to separate Horizon Worlds and related branding from the Quest platform, which began earlier this year . If you're unfamiliar, Meta Horizon+ is the company's $8/month (or $60/year) subscription service for its VR devices. Subscribers get access to a Games Catalog of around 50 major VR titles, as well as an Indie Catalog of around 50 smaller titles, for a total of around 100 games. In February 2026, Meta reported that the subscription service had crossed 1 million "active subscribers" in 2025 . In July, the company also added a starter edition of Xbox Game Pass to Horizon+, giving subscribers access to 50+ games and 10 hours of cloud gaming each month. More recently, the service has started regularly offering subscribers exclusive game discounts and free add-ons for games. Adding 3D movies to Horizon+ would align with the media focus of Meta VR Glasses and recent Horizon OS updates , as well as the strategy outlined by Meta Director of Games Chris Pruett at GDC in March. Pruett stated that the company expects "more Mainstream Adults to enter VR through media consumption first, then discover games once they are in-headset" over the next couple of years. sources.title: Who is Alice Huang? Chinese businesswoman at centre of Nvidia spy scandal
passages: Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused by US intelligence agencies of working for Beijing, has emerged at the centre of a major controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

She eventually became a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a data centre company that provides AI computing infrastructure to businesses, including major Chinese technology firms.According to The New York Times, Megaspeed began making multibillion-dollar purchases of advanced Nvidia chips around 2024.

The company reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia processors over two years, making it one of the chipmaker's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.Huang is also understood to have developed connections with senior executives across the AI chip industry.

This arrangement could potentially provide Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips despite US restrictions on direct sales to China.US authorities have also examined whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies circumvent export restrictions.

Megaspeed has said its current leadership takes the claims seriously and has appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.Nvidia, meanwhile, has defended Jensen Huang's interactions with the businesswoman, describing them as normal customer engagements.

However, the company has maintained that it has no reason to believe its trade secrets or US national security were compromised.From television reporter to a top executive at MegaspeedAlice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who previously worked as a television reporter in China before moving into the technology and business sector.

extraction.body: Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused by US intelligence agencies of working for Beijing, has emerged at the centre of a major controversy involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. According to a report by The New York Times, China's Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on the chipmaker's chief executive and potentially influence the company's decisions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chip sales to China.The allegations have prompted Nvidia's board to launch an independent investigation after reports that Jensen Huang, 63, had developed a close relationship with the businesswoman. The Nvidia chief has separately admitted to being unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. However, the company has maintained that it has no reason to believe its trade secrets or US national security were compromised.From television reporter to a top executive at MegaspeedAlice Huang, also known as Huang Le, is a Chinese citizen who previously worked as a television reporter in China before moving into the technology and business sector. She eventually became a senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a data centre company that provides AI computing infrastructure to businesses, including major Chinese technology firms.According to The New York Times, Megaspeed began making multibillion-dollar purchases of advanced Nvidia chips around 2024. The company reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia processors over two years, making it one of the chipmaker's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.Huang is also understood to have developed connections with senior executives across the AI chip industry. She attended technology conferences and private business dinners and had professional links with leaders at companies involved in assembling Nvidia-powered supercomputers.The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had monitored her communications for at least a year before concluding that she was working for China's Ministry of State Security (MSS). A classified intelligence assessment circulated among senior Trump administration officials reportedly identified her as an asset recruited to collect information on Jensen Huang.US intelligence agencies determined that Alice Huang, pictured drinking whiskey and dining with the tech mogul, was secretly passing information to Beijing, the newspaper reported.The report also said electronic surveillance identified Jensen Huang as one of her contacts. The two are not related.Intelligence operation and Megaspeed's China linksAccording to the intelligence assessment cited by The New York Times, Beijing's objective was potentially to gain insights into Nvidia's operations and influence its position on allowing China access to advanced AI processors.Megaspeed's business model has also come under scrutiny. The company reportedly built data centres across Southeast Asia and rented computing power to Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba. This arrangement could potentially provide Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips despite US restrictions on direct sales to China.US authorities have also examined whether Megaspeed helped Chinese companies circumvent export restrictions. The New York Times reported that the network of businesses and investors connected to Huang had links to companies in Shanghai and Zhejiang, as well as financial connections to China's military technology establishment.Alice Huang has not publicly responded to the allegations or multiple requests for comment. Megaspeed has said its current leadership takes the claims seriously and has appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.Nvidia, meanwhile, has defended Jensen Huang's interactions with the businesswoman, describing them as normal customer engagements. A company spokesperson said the CEO regularly meets thousands of customer executives and that such interactions do not involve sensitive trade secrets.You use AI every day.

extraction.body: Alice Huang's ties to Megaspeed drew scrutiny over alleged Nvidia chip transfers to China, while her whereabouts remain unknown. More details have emerged about Alice Huang, the Singapore-based executive U.S. officials allege was collecting intelligence on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for China. He has acknowledged the affair. Beijing denies the spying claims. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair in a memo to Nvidia employees on Sunday. The company’s board opened an independent investigation the same day into reports that foreign intelligence targeted him. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” Jensen Huang wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” Alice Huang, who also goes by her Chinese name Huang Le, was a reporter for Chinese state media nearly two decades ago, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday. She later moved into finance, working for HSBC and Chinese financial companies, the newspaper said. A profile on Simuwang, a Chinese private fund database, lists her as a former reporter for state broadcaster China Central Television and regional broadcaster Hunan TV. The profile says she went on to work as an assistant to the head of HSBC’s private banking division and as a vice president at Citic Securities. She then became executive director of Shanghai Hexi Investment. None of the career claims have been independently confirmed. A Hunan TV executive told the New York Post that the broadcaster had never heard of her, and the Post found no reporter profile under her name on the websites of either broadcaster. HSBC and Citic Securities did not respond to the Post’s requests for comment. Alice Huang became an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company, in 2023. Singapore’s corporate registry shows she served as a director from March to November that year, the Journal reported. Fluent in English, she built wide connections with senior executives across the chip industry. Alice Huang first met Jensen Huang at an annual Nvidia event in California in early 2024, where she represented Megaspeed, people familiar with the matter told the Journal. The two met again that June in Taipei around Computex 2024, Taiwan’s biggest tech trade show. After the show, they drank whiskey with other tech executives at a Taipei bar. A photo of the gathering posted on LinkedIn by NetThunder, an Nvidia business partner, shows Alice Huang in glittering jewelry seated next to Jensen Huang. Video and photos from a dinner at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex 2025 show the two kissing each other on the cheek and leaving in the same car, the Journal reported. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, who presented herself as a Megaspeed executive, is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. The New York Times first reported on Oct. 29 that officials had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. A memo written by U.S. officials earlier this year described the two as romantically involved, the Financial Times reported last week. Officials in Singapore and Taiwan who investigated her ties to China suspected that Chinese intelligence recruited her after learning of her closeness to the Nvidia chief, the Journal reported last month. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs later said it had conducted no such investigation into Alice Huang. Alice Huang’s whereabouts are unknown. Two people in contact with her earlier this year said she was in China at the time, the Journal reported. She has left Megaspeed, which is still operating. Questions about the relationship surfaced six months ago. Short seller Culper Research said in a May report that Jensen Huang had vouched for Megaspeed while maintaining an “uncomfortably close relationship” with Alice Huang. Megaspeed became the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia within three years of its founding. It imported at least $4.6 billion worth of Nvidia hardware from its 2023 launch through November 2025, Bloomberg reported last December based on Malaysian and Indonesian customs data. Washington has been investigating whether the company helped funnel Nvidia chips to China in breach of export controls. The Commerce Department opened a probe in late 2024, and the Justice Department is now investigating, the Journal reported. Megaspeed said in a LinkedIn statement that investigations had found no evidence of illicit chip transfers or other illegal activity. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” John Rizzo, an Nvidia spokesperson, said after the Times report. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.” The company has also said allegations that Megaspeed diverted chips to China were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year. “The reports are baseless and purely slanderous smears against China,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry, said on Oct. 30. The government will add three physical AI-related industries to its flagship growth initiative, expanding financial, tax and regulatory support. AI-generated videos and memes pairing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with Alice Huang spread online after his infidelity admission. Nvidia says its board sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised, but will review all available information with Huang’s cooperation. 민주당이 미 의회 상·하원에서 모두 과반을 차지하면서 한국의 대미 투자·관세 합의가 새로운 불확실성에 직면했다. 이번 선거 결과로 합의 이행에 필요한 의회 지원을 얻기가 어려워질 수 있다는 분석이다.

extraction.body: Alice Huang's ties to Megaspeed drew scrutiny over alleged Nvidia chip transfers to China, while her whereabouts remain unknown. More details have emerged about Alice Huang, the Singapore-based executive U.S. officials allege was collecting intelligence on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for China. He has acknowledged the affair. Beijing denies the spying claims. Jensen Huang admitted to the affair in a memo to Nvidia employees on Sunday. The company’s board opened an independent investigation the same day into reports that foreign intelligence targeted him. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” Jensen Huang wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” Alice Huang, who also goes by her Chinese name Huang Le, was a reporter for Chinese state media nearly two decades ago, The Wall Street Journal reported Monday. She later moved into finance, working for HSBC and Chinese financial companies, the newspaper said. A profile on Simuwang, a Chinese private fund database, lists her as a former reporter for state broadcaster China Central Television and regional broadcaster Hunan TV. The profile says she went on to work as an assistant to the head of HSBC’s private banking division and as a vice president at Citic Securities. She then became executive director of Shanghai Hexi Investment. None of the career claims have been independently confirmed. A Hunan TV executive told the New York Post that the broadcaster had never heard of her, and the Post found no reporter profile under her name on the websites of either broadcaster. HSBC and Citic Securities did not respond to the Post’s requests for comment. Alice Huang became an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data center company, in 2023. Singapore’s corporate registry shows she served as a director from March to November that year, the Journal reported. Fluent in English, she built wide connections with senior executives across the chip industry. Alice Huang first met Jensen Huang at an annual Nvidia event in California in early 2024, where she represented Megaspeed, people familiar with the matter told the Journal. The two met again that June in Taipei around Computex 2024, Taiwan’s biggest tech trade show. After the show, they drank whiskey with other tech executives at a Taipei bar. A photo of the gathering posted on LinkedIn by NetThunder, an Nvidia business partner, shows Alice Huang in glittering jewelry seated next to Jensen Huang. Video and photos from a dinner at a Chinese restaurant in Taipei during Computex 2025 show the two kissing each other on the cheek and leaving in the same car, the Journal reported. U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, who presented herself as a Megaspeed executive, is a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. The New York Times first reported on Oct. 29 that officials had concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. A memo written by U.S. officials earlier this year described the two as romantically involved, the Financial Times reported last week. Officials in Singapore and Taiwan who investigated her ties to China suspected that Chinese intelligence recruited her after learning of her closeness to the Nvidia chief, the Journal reported last month. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs later said it had conducted no such investigation into Alice Huang. Alice Huang’s whereabouts are unknown. Two people in contact with her earlier this year said she was in China at the time, the Journal reported. She has left Megaspeed, which is still operating. Questions about the relationship surfaced six months ago. Short seller Culper Research said in a May report that Jensen Huang had vouched for Megaspeed while maintaining an “uncomfortably close relationship” with Alice Huang. Megaspeed became the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia within three years of its founding. It imported at least $4.6 billion worth of Nvidia hardware from its 2023 launch through November 2025, Bloomberg reported last December based on Malaysian and Indonesian customs data. Washington has been investigating whether the company helped funnel Nvidia chips to China in breach of export controls. The Commerce Department opened a probe in late 2024, and the Justice Department is now investigating, the Journal reported. Megaspeed said in a LinkedIn statement that investigations had found no evidence of illicit chip transfers or other illegal activity. “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” John Rizzo, an Nvidia spokesperson, said after the Times report. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.” The company has also said allegations that Megaspeed diverted chips to China were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year. “The reports are baseless and purely slanderous smears against China,” Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry, said on Oct. 30. The government will add three physical AI-related industries to its flagship growth initiative, expanding financial, tax and regulatory support. AI-generated videos and memes pairing Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with Alice Huang spread online after his infidelity admission. Nvidia says its board sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised, but will review all available information with Huang’s cooperation. 민주당이 미 의회 상·하원에서 모두 과반을 차지하면서 한국의 대미 투자·관세 합의가 새로운 불확실성에 직면했다. 이번 선거 결과로 합의 이행에 필요한 의회 지원을 얻기가 어려워질 수 있다는 분석이다.

sources.title: US calls for new Europe security at Russia-Ukraine talks - RTE.ie
passages: At the Abu Dhabi talks, Mr Trump's son-in-law Kushner said the United States hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace".

Ukraine has warned against a "Yalta 2.0", referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union after World War II, and the EU has said security arrangements can only be discussed after a ceasefire.
Europe has been rattled as Mr Trump has floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security, also worrying that Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat.

In a sign it is serious about reviving its demand to review Europe's decades-old security arrangement, Russia included a diplomat - Sergei Ryabkov - who logged Moscow's pre-invasion demand for NATO to pull back from eastern Europe.
"Allowing Russia to decide the borders of Europe will be a huge mistake," Denmark's Mette Frederiksen said, as she hosted Mr Zelensky.

Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky later said the talks were "constructive and quite substantive", saying his team reported to him that humanitarian issues and security guarantees were among what was discussed.
Speaking in Copenhagen, the Ukrainian president also said it was "time" for Europe to choose a representative for the talks.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, United States and NATO reaffirmed their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture".
NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part.

The EU last year came up with a €90bn loan for Ukraine, but as Russia has stepped up its bombardments of Ukraine's infrastructure, it has become increasingly clear that those funds will run out before the end of next year.
\u003Cp\u003EVolodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine\u0027s leverage in the talks was increasing\u003C/p\u003E
Russia, which occupies swathes of its smaller neighbour, pummelled Ukraine with more attacks overnight, cutting power to thousands as temperatures plummet.

extraction.body: A first day of US-led talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi ended with Washington calling for a "new" security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent's future. Mr Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff brought together the warring sides for several hours of negotiations - the first since February - that are set to continue tomorrow. In Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the talks as "very productive" and called for Europeans to be eventually included at the negotiating table "because they are part of solving this problem". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky later said the talks were "constructive and quite substantive", saying his team reported to him that humanitarian issues and security guarantees were among what was discussed. Speaking in Copenhagen, the Ukrainian president also said it was "time" for Europe to choose a representative for the talks. Europe has been rattled as Mr Trump has floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe's post-war security, also worrying that Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat. At the Abu Dhabi talks, Mr Trump's son-in-law Kushner said the United States hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that will secure "decades, if not centuries, of peace". Moscow, which several weeks before invading Ukraine issued an ultimatum to Western countries to roll back troops from eastern Europe, had also said this was a priority. Ukraine has warned against a "Yalta 2.0", referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the Soviet Union after World War II, and the EU has said security arrangements can only be discussed after a ceasefire. "Putin wants the USSR back," Mr Zelensky told Danish media. Russia, which occupies swathes of its smaller neighbour, pummelled Ukraine with more attacks overnight, cutting power to thousands as temperatures plummet. Mr Putin has repeatedly turned down broader ceasefire offers and vowed his troops will press on in Ukraine. A Russian delegation source had said that settling the war was "merely one item on the agenda" and that Moscow's main objective was reviewing security "for the entire continent". Kyiv's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov met the US envoys and European, EU and NATO officials before the negotiations. NATO's general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part. In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, United States and NATO reaffirmed their "shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture". Mr Umerov said Kyiv's priorities remained securing a ceasefire and security guarantees. "Our people are waiting to end this war," he said. As talks continued, Ukrainian and French foreign ministers in Paris commended US efforts to push for "partial truces", which could serve as a "first step toward a complete and unconditional ceasefire". Last month, a local truce in Ukraine's Kherson region brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump became the longest pause in fighting during the war. Kyiv is also pushing post-war support for its army. The Ukrainian leader is due to meet other Nordic leaders in Denmark and earlier spoke to Finland's Alexander Stubb, telling him Kyiv's negotiators are doing their "best" to ensure talks "deliver results". sources.title: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect
passages: New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws.
The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027.

It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports.
On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University.
The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks.
Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital.
The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed.

Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm.
Illinois’ SB 315, which will go into effect at the start of 2027, has similar requirements, plus includes independent safety compliance audits.

extraction.body: New York is gearing up to enforce one of the country’s most significant AI safety laws. The state opened a registration portal Tuesday, with which large frontier AI developers like Anthropic and OpenAI will be required to register by January 1, 2027. The RAISE Act , New York’s safety and transparency bill, kicks in at the start of the year. It mandates that large frontier developers — companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue — have to publish safety frameworks on their websites, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, and issue public model transparency reports. The newly formed Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT) will implement the RAISE Act and oversee large frontier AI labs. Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. The state also can bring enforcement actions against companies that fail to register with the new portal, though a spokesperson declined to provide specifics. “Tech moguls tell us that their vision for AI is inevitable,” Governor Kathy Hochul said Tuesday during a press briefing. “They tell us get on board or get left behind… That any collateral damage is worth it as long as we win the race to the AI cliff.” On Tuesday, Hochul also launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research based at State University of New York’s Binghamton University. The center will independently evaluate the safety, security, and operation of advanced AI systems and work with DIGIT to review companies’ safety frameworks. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. “We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said. The RAISE Act isn’t the only safety law New York has passed. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm. extraction.body: New York just became the first state to enforce comprehensive AI safety regulations on the industry's biggest players. The state's RAISE Act takes effect today, forcing OpenAI and Anthropic to register with regulators, disclose their safety practices, and report critical incidents or face financial penalties. The timing couldn't be more pointed - Anthropic is days away from its IPO, while OpenAI races to monetize ChatGPT through new business features. OpenAI and Anthropic just got their first taste of serious state-level regulation. New York's RAISE Act - short for Responsible AI Safety and Enforcement - officially takes effect today, establishing the most comprehensive state-level oversight framework for artificial intelligence development in the country. The law requires major AI developers to register with New York regulators, publicly disclose their safety testing practices, and report any critical incidents involving their systems. Companies that fail to comply face financial penalties, though the exact fine structure remains under regulatory review. New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the bill into law earlier this year, positioning the state as the first to move beyond voluntary AI safety commitments. The timing hits particularly hard for Anthropic, which priced its IPO at $70-78 per share just days ago ahead of its November 19 public debut. The company has been on a product blitz this week, launching Claude Meetings and shipping new Mythos and Fable models to demonstrate momentum before going public. The company just transformed ChatGPT into a business discovery engine, letting companies create profiles and listings inside the chatbot as it pivots hard toward commerce. That expansion into new use cases means more surface area for regulators to scrutinize, and New York's law specifically targets systems capable of general-purpose reasoning - exactly what ChatGPT does. The RAISE Act focuses on what regulators call "advanced AI systems" - models with broad capabilities across multiple domains that could pose systemic risks. Companies must file detailed disclosures about their model architectures, training data sources, safety testing protocols, and incident response procedures. The law also mandates ongoing reporting - if a registered AI system causes or contributes to a critical incident, developers have 72 hours to notify state authorities with a preliminary assessment. The law defines it broadly: any malfunction, misuse, or unexpected behavior that results in significant harm to individuals, critical infrastructure, or public safety. If New York's enforcement goes smoothly, expect a wave of copycat legislation across blue states by mid-2027. The federal government remains conspicuously absent from AI safety regulation despite years of hand-wringing. That vacuum let New York move first, but it also creates a patchwork compliance problem for companies operating nationally. OpenAI and Anthropic now face the prospect of navigating 50 different state regulatory frameworks if this trend accelerates. Neither company has issued public statements about New York's enforcement deadline, though both have previously expressed support for "thoughtful regulation" in congressional testimony. New York's Department of Financial Services will oversee compliance, but the agency hasn't disclosed how many investigators it's assigned to AI oversight or what its audit schedule looks like. Without serious enforcement teeth, the RAISE Act risks becoming another box-checking exercise that companies navigate with minimal operational changes. AI developers can no longer treat safety as a purely voluntary exercise or a marketing talking point. New York's RAISE Act enforcement marks the end of AI's self-regulation era and the beginning of a messy, state-by-state compliance landscape. For OpenAI and Anthropic, the immediate burden is manageable - file paperwork, document existing safety practices, set up incident reporting. Every state that follows New York's lead adds complexity, cost, and legal risk. Either way, the days of building AI systems without regulatory oversight just ended.

sources.title: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled - PBS
passages: The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI recently declared America's cutting-edge models are so powerful, they're dangerous, and need to be regulated and independently tested before being released.
In a rare instance of unity, they have sketched alarming scenarios in essays, social media posts and speeches to the United Nations.
OpenAI representatives told reporters recently that they have talked with AI companies including Anthropic and Google about pausing development.
They also argue they need independent auditors to check the labs' progress, if the government won't regulate.

Stosz now works at one such evaluation lab that has worked with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to test their systems, and also chairs the AI Evaluator Forum, which is drafting best practices for the field.
He said even the forum has questions about what Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman want.

"Lots of evaluators are interested in embedding with labs and getting greater access, but it's a little ambiguous what embedded evaluators means," said Stosz, now head of governance at Transluce, which revealed last week that OpenAI agents hacked U.S. and Australian government websites.
"Will evaluators be able to thoroughly investigate, assuming that access is granted in a way that does not undermine their independence and credibility?"

Those aims may not exactly align with what Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon sought when he quit via a post on X this month, calling for a pause on tech development to keep "superhuman" systems from eluding their makers' control.

But the companies saw his post as an opportunity to highlight their own safety efforts and position themselves as cautious market leaders, just when they need fresh capital before going public on Wall Street.

Daniel Kokotajlo, who left OpenAI in 2024 over concerns similar to Coxon's, said he continues to worry that AI systems are advancing faster than companies can control, and fears existential scenarios such as AI's potential to supercharge the creation of bioweapons, nuclear war or other catastrophes.

Turning the conversation toward unproven threats — and away from polarizing issues such as data centers' environmental impacts, uncontrolled hacking incidents, mass AI-powered surveillance and the AI systems' use in warfare — puts Silicon Valley in a more comfortable position, said Sarah Shoker, who previously led OpenAI's geopolitics team.

The agency still exists, but the field has since expanded to include an array of independent evaluation firms, such as Berkeley, California-based nonprofit METR, which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested in a recent essay could help vet his company's safety practices.

The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI recently declared America's cutting-edge models are so powerful, they're dangerous, and need to be regulated and independently tested before being released. In a rare instance of unity, they have sketched alarming scenarios in essays, social media posts and speeches to the United Nations. Along the way, they are shaping the conversation around how their technology should be controlled. With their rhetoric, the companies appear to be seeking public favor and to set the terms for their own safety protocols in the unregulated market, experts, analysts and former government evaluators told The Associated Press. Those aims may not exactly align with what Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon sought when he quit via a post on X this month, calling for a pause on tech development to keep "superhuman" systems from eluding their makers' control. But the companies saw his post as an opportunity to highlight their own safety efforts and position themselves as cautious market leaders, just when they need fresh capital before going public on Wall Street. President Donald Trump has shunned the need for new AI regulations, dismissing talk of risks to humanity as a "HOAX" designed to help China. An Anthropic spokesperson said in response to questions for this story that the company has been calling for regulation for several years. An OpenAI spokesperson, Liz Bourgeois, noted the company recently paused training of its most advanced models. "People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves," Bourgeois said. Turning the conversation toward unproven threats — and away from polarizing issues such as data centers' environmental impacts, uncontrolled hacking incidents, mass AI-powered surveillance and the AI systems' use in warfare — puts Silicon Valley in a more comfortable position, said Sarah Shoker, who previously led OpenAI's geopolitics team. "Once again we're talking about existential risk, while deprioritizing a number of other safety-critical risks that exist today. If you look at the use of AI in military tech, you can see that these systems are already used to kill people," said Shoker, a senior non-resident fellow at University of California, Berkeley Risk & Security Lab. As AI companies have gone from building chatbots to advanced AI "world models" with 3D awareness, debate has raged over how their technologies should be tested. Problematic incidents have shown leading AI companies failing to police themselves or design safe experiments. In recent months, leading labs' AI agents have hacked into external websites after being allowed to escape company training sandboxes, interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, and appeared to achieve a mathematical breakthrough only to face accusations of stealing mathematicians' work. OpenAI representatives told reporters recently that they have talked with AI companies including Anthropic and Google about pausing development. They also argue they need independent auditors to check the labs' progress, if the government won't regulate. Trump has shown little interest in regulating AI, which has been a major driver of recent U.S. economic growth. The Republican president himself has struck deals with Silicon Valley firms that more closely tie the economy to their successes. San Francisco venture capitalist David Sacks, who co-chairs Trump's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, has dismissed calls for an AI slowdown as fearmongering from the "Doomer Industrial Complex." The reality is the Trump administration already evaluates some of the tech giants' models through a little-known federal agency, the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Democratic President Joe Biden created the agency in 2023, when it was heralded as a clearinghouse for labs to voluntarily submit advanced AI models for testing. The agency still exists, but the field has since expanded to include an array of independent evaluation firms, such as Berkeley, California-based nonprofit METR, which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested in a recent essay could help vet his company's safety practices. But unlike regulated sectors like restaurants, financial services or aviation, there are no universal standards for how to test the safety and security of AI systems, said Andrew Strait, who recently left the United Kingdom's AI Security Institute, which worked with CAISI. Notably, the companies aren't calling for more oversight from the government agency equipped to handle such requests, said Conrad Stosz, who previously led CAISI. Instead, they're vowing to create their own auditing parameters and choose particular evaluators to grade them. Stosz now works at one such evaluation lab that has worked with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to test their systems, and also chairs the AI Evaluator Forum, which is drafting best practices for the field. He said even the forum has questions about what Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman want. "Lots of evaluators are interested in embedding with labs and getting greater access, but it's a little ambiguous what embedded evaluators means," said Stosz, now head of governance at Transluce, which revealed last week that OpenAI agents hacked U.S. and Australian government websites. "Will evaluators be able to thoroughly investigate, assuming that access is granted in a way that does not undermine their independence and credibility?" For Harrison Rolfes, a PitchBook senior research analyst, AI companies' calls for caution seem meant to curry favor with investors ahead of public offerings and the midterms, when the political winds could shift. Democratic governors already are rushing to show they're taking the warnings seriously. Meanwhile, the AI giants can block smaller competitors' growth by positioning themselves as the safest bet for investors, as well as for AI chipmakers and tech companies such as Nvidia and Google, which in turn can benefit from deals that provide the giant AI companies compute power, Rolfes said. "They're creating a wall or a moat within this sector. … It's genius and they're all going to make a lot of money," Rolfes said. "That's where I see this heading, having the top companies in the world just creating their own wall, and then using the safety as the reason." Not all AI companies endorse a slowdown. Chipmaker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang said in a phone conversation with Trump — a call he took onstage at a conference — that he agrees there has been excessive AI alarmism and companies can choose to pace themselves. Daniel Kokotajlo, who left OpenAI in 2024 over concerns similar to Coxon's, said he continues to worry that AI systems are advancing faster than companies can control, and fears existential scenarios such as AI's potential to supercharge the creation of bioweapons, nuclear war or other catastrophes. "All of this talk is actually a way to sort of dissipate and redirect this political will that has built up, rather than actually channeling that political will to do something good," said Kokotajlo, who now leads an AI safety advocacy organization and said he counseled Coxon before he resigned. "Just please don't do the thing that's going to get us all killed." AP writer Josh Boak in Washington contributed to this report. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Photo by Brendan McDermid/Reuters

Penalties can be as high as $1 million for one violation and $3 million for subsequent violations. Hochul first announced the center in January with $55 million in donations and capital. “We’re building a national model for smart, sensible AI regulation, a model that puts communities above corporations and people above powerful technology,” Hochul said. Last year, the state began enforcing a law that requires AI companion operators to regularly let users know they’re talking to a bot, and to make reasonable efforts to detect suicidal ideation and self-harm.
