sources.title: Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled - PBS
passages: The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI recently declared America's cutting-edge models are so powerful, they're dangerous, and need to be regulated and independently tested before being released.
In a rare instance of unity, they have sketched alarming scenarios in essays, social media posts and speeches to the United Nations.
OpenAI representatives told reporters recently that they have talked with AI companies including Anthropic and Google about pausing development.
They also argue they need independent auditors to check the labs' progress, if the government won't regulate.

Stosz now works at one such evaluation lab that has worked with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to test their systems, and also chairs the AI Evaluator Forum, which is drafting best practices for the field.
He said even the forum has questions about what Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman want.

"Lots of evaluators are interested in embedding with labs and getting greater access, but it's a little ambiguous what embedded evaluators means," said Stosz, now head of governance at Transluce, which revealed last week that OpenAI agents hacked U.S. and Australian government websites.
"Will evaluators be able to thoroughly investigate, assuming that access is granted in a way that does not undermine their independence and credibility?"

Those aims may not exactly align with what Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon sought when he quit via a post on X this month, calling for a pause on tech development to keep "superhuman" systems from eluding their makers' control.

But the companies saw his post as an opportunity to highlight their own safety efforts and position themselves as cautious market leaders, just when they need fresh capital before going public on Wall Street.

Daniel Kokotajlo, who left OpenAI in 2024 over concerns similar to Coxon's, said he continues to worry that AI systems are advancing faster than companies can control, and fears existential scenarios such as AI's potential to supercharge the creation of bioweapons, nuclear war or other catastrophes.

Turning the conversation toward unproven threats — and away from polarizing issues such as data centers' environmental impacts, uncontrolled hacking incidents, mass AI-powered surveillance and the AI systems' use in warfare — puts Silicon Valley in a more comfortable position, said Sarah Shoker, who previously led OpenAI's geopolitics team.

The agency still exists, but the field has since expanded to include an array of independent evaluation firms, such as Berkeley, California-based nonprofit METR, which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested in a recent essay could help vet his company's safety practices.

The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI recently declared America's cutting-edge models are so powerful, they're dangerous, and need to be regulated and independently tested before being released. In a rare instance of unity, they have sketched alarming scenarios in essays, social media posts and speeches to the United Nations. Along the way, they are shaping the conversation around how their technology should be controlled. With their rhetoric, the companies appear to be seeking public favor and to set the terms for their own safety protocols in the unregulated market, experts, analysts and former government evaluators told The Associated Press. Those aims may not exactly align with what Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon sought when he quit via a post on X this month, calling for a pause on tech development to keep "superhuman" systems from eluding their makers' control. But the companies saw his post as an opportunity to highlight their own safety efforts and position themselves as cautious market leaders, just when they need fresh capital before going public on Wall Street. President Donald Trump has shunned the need for new AI regulations, dismissing talk of risks to humanity as a "HOAX" designed to help China. An Anthropic spokesperson said in response to questions for this story that the company has been calling for regulation for several years. An OpenAI spokesperson, Liz Bourgeois, noted the company recently paused training of its most advanced models. "People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves," Bourgeois said. Turning the conversation toward unproven threats — and away from polarizing issues such as data centers' environmental impacts, uncontrolled hacking incidents, mass AI-powered surveillance and the AI systems' use in warfare — puts Silicon Valley in a more comfortable position, said Sarah Shoker, who previously led OpenAI's geopolitics team. "Once again we're talking about existential risk, while deprioritizing a number of other safety-critical risks that exist today. If you look at the use of AI in military tech, you can see that these systems are already used to kill people," said Shoker, a senior non-resident fellow at University of California, Berkeley Risk & Security Lab. As AI companies have gone from building chatbots to advanced AI "world models" with 3D awareness, debate has raged over how their technologies should be tested. Problematic incidents have shown leading AI companies failing to police themselves or design safe experiments. In recent months, leading labs' AI agents have hacked into external websites after being allowed to escape company training sandboxes, interacted with U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, and appeared to achieve a mathematical breakthrough only to face accusations of stealing mathematicians' work. OpenAI representatives told reporters recently that they have talked with AI companies including Anthropic and Google about pausing development. They also argue they need independent auditors to check the labs' progress, if the government won't regulate. Trump has shown little interest in regulating AI, which has been a major driver of recent U.S. economic growth. The Republican president himself has struck deals with Silicon Valley firms that more closely tie the economy to their successes. San Francisco venture capitalist David Sacks, who co-chairs Trump's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, has dismissed calls for an AI slowdown as fearmongering from the "Doomer Industrial Complex." The reality is the Trump administration already evaluates some of the tech giants' models through a little-known federal agency, the U.S. Center for AI Standards and Innovation. Democratic President Joe Biden created the agency in 2023, when it was heralded as a clearinghouse for labs to voluntarily submit advanced AI models for testing. The agency still exists, but the field has since expanded to include an array of independent evaluation firms, such as Berkeley, California-based nonprofit METR, which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested in a recent essay could help vet his company's safety practices. But unlike regulated sectors like restaurants, financial services or aviation, there are no universal standards for how to test the safety and security of AI systems, said Andrew Strait, who recently left the United Kingdom's AI Security Institute, which worked with CAISI. Notably, the companies aren't calling for more oversight from the government agency equipped to handle such requests, said Conrad Stosz, who previously led CAISI. Instead, they're vowing to create their own auditing parameters and choose particular evaluators to grade them. Stosz now works at one such evaluation lab that has worked with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to test their systems, and also chairs the AI Evaluator Forum, which is drafting best practices for the field. He said even the forum has questions about what Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman want. "Lots of evaluators are interested in embedding with labs and getting greater access, but it's a little ambiguous what embedded evaluators means," said Stosz, now head of governance at Transluce, which revealed last week that OpenAI agents hacked U.S. and Australian government websites. "Will evaluators be able to thoroughly investigate, assuming that access is granted in a way that does not undermine their independence and credibility?" For Harrison Rolfes, a PitchBook senior research analyst, AI companies' calls for caution seem meant to curry favor with investors ahead of public offerings and the midterms, when the political winds could shift. Democratic governors already are rushing to show they're taking the warnings seriously. Meanwhile, the AI giants can block smaller competitors' growth by positioning themselves as the safest bet for investors, as well as for AI chipmakers and tech companies such as Nvidia and Google, which in turn can benefit from deals that provide the giant AI companies compute power, Rolfes said. "They're creating a wall or a moat within this sector. … It's genius and they're all going to make a lot of money," Rolfes said. "That's where I see this heading, having the top companies in the world just creating their own wall, and then using the safety as the reason." Not all AI companies endorse a slowdown. Chipmaker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang said in a phone conversation with Trump — a call he took onstage at a conference — that he agrees there has been excessive AI alarmism and companies can choose to pace themselves. Daniel Kokotajlo, who left OpenAI in 2024 over concerns similar to Coxon's, said he continues to worry that AI systems are advancing faster than companies can control, and fears existential scenarios such as AI's potential to supercharge the creation of bioweapons, nuclear war or other catastrophes. "All of this talk is actually a way to sort of dissipate and redirect this political will that has built up, rather than actually channeling that political will to do something good," said Kokotajlo, who now leads an AI safety advocacy organization and said he counseled Coxon before he resigned. "Just please don't do the thing that's going to get us all killed." AP writer Josh Boak in Washington contributed to this report. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Left: Clement Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face, and Dario Amodei co-founder of Anthropic address the United Nations Security Council via video link during a Wednesday session on Artificial Intelligence during the 81st United Nations General Assembly, at UN Headquarters in New York City. Photo by Brendan McDermid/Reuters

Cryptocurrency markets took another hit on Tuesday, November 10, as hotter-than-expected inflation data weighed on investor sentiment and fueled concerns about higher interest rates. As of early evening, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) fell 1.83% to $73,874.38, while Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) declined 3.43% to $2,059.16 and Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) dropped 3.69% to $83.37. The broad-based sell-off reflected weakening risk appetite as investors reassessed the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy. Tuesday's inflation surprise triggered a sharp sell-off in U.S. government bonds, pushing Treasury yields higher as investors priced in more aggressive monetary tightening. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5%, while the more policy-sensitive two-year yield climbed toward 4.75%. Higher yields make fixed-income investments more attractive relative to speculative assets, creating additional headwinds for cryptocurrencies. The U.S. dollar also strengthened, with the dollar index gaining approximately 0.5%. A stronger dollar can weigh on dollar-denominated assets like Bitcoin by tightening global financial conditions and reducing purchasing power for overseas investors. Meanwhile, markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December, with some traders considering the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point increase. Together, rising bond yields, a stronger dollar, and tighter monetary policy expectations are creating an increasingly challenging backdrop for digital assets. Spot Bitcoin ETFs traded lower, with iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (NASDAQ:IBIT) down 1.51% and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (NYSEMKT:FBTC) down 1.49%. Spot Ether funds also weakened, as iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (NASDAQ:ETHA) fell 3.27%. Bitcoin's struggle to hold $74,000 raises concerns about the strength of underlying demand. extraction.body: Bitcoin dropped below $74,000 on November 10, 2026, after October US inflation beat forecasts. Traders now see an 89% chance of a Fed rate increase on December 9. Solana, XRP and Ethereum fell more than Bitcoin, and about $360 million in crypto bets were liquidated. Bitcoin fell below $74,000 on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, trading near $73,660, after hotter-than-expected US inflation data led traders to raise their bets on a Federal Reserve interest rate increase next month. Solana, Ethereum and XRP fell harder than Bitcoin, which is the focus of the latest crypto selloff. Bitcoin was down 1.3% over 24 hours. The drop took it under the roughly $75,700 low it hit on election night last week. Retail sentiment on the Stocktwits platform stayed in bearish territory over the past day. The consumer price index, a measure of what households pay for goods and services, rose 0.4% in October from September. Economists had expected 0.3%. Prices had climbed 0.6% in September. Core CPI strips out food and energy, which tend to swing more. It rose 0.3%, against a 0.2% forecast. The report carried no annual inflation figures. The 2025 government shutdown disrupted the collection of price data a year earlier. Traders now see an 89% chance that the Fed raises rates by a quarter point at its December 9 meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool. That would lift the federal funds rate to a range of 4% to 4.25%. They put an 11% chance on a larger half-point increase. A week ago the picture was softer. After the midterm elections, markets gave about a 70% probability to any rate increase in December. Higher rates tend to weigh on assets such as cryptocurrencies, which pay no interest. Solana dropped more than 3% in 24 hours to around $84. XRP, the token tied to Ripple, fell about 3% to $1.06. Ethereum, the largest altcoin (any crypto other than Bitcoin), lost around 2.8% to roughly $2,000. The whole crypto market shed about 1.8% over the same period. It is under threat of slipping below $2.5 trillion in total value. The slide forced out leveraged traders. A liquidation happens when an exchange closes a borrowed-money bet because the trader can no longer cover losses. About $200 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the hour after the inflation report. More than $179 million of that came from long positions, which are bets on rising prices. Across the past 24 hours, liquidations totaled about $360 million. Of that, $282 million was bullish bets. The English-language global edition of JournalArta.

Cryptocurrency markets took another hit on Tuesday, November 10, as hotter-than-expected inflation data weighed on investor sentiment and fueled concerns about higher interest rates. As of early evening, Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) fell 1.83% to $73,874.38, while Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH) declined 3.43% to $2,059.16 and Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) dropped 3.69% to $83.37. The broad-based sell-off reflected weakening risk appetite as investors reassessed the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.

Tuesday's inflation surprise triggered a sharp sell-off in U.S. government bonds, pushing Treasury yields higher as investors priced in more aggressive monetary tightening. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5%, while the more policy-sensitive two-year yield climbed toward 4.75%. Higher yields make fixed-income investments more attractive relative to speculative assets, creating additional headwinds for cryptocurrencies.

The U.S. dollar also strengthened, with the dollar index gaining approximately 0.5%. A stronger dollar can weigh on dollar-denominated assets like Bitcoin by tightening global financial conditions and reducing purchasing power for overseas investors.

Meanwhile, markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December, with some traders considering the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point increase. Together, rising bond yields, a stronger dollar, and tighter monetary policy expectations are creating an increasingly challenging backdrop for digital assets.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs traded lower, with iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (NASDAQ:IBIT) down 1.51% and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (NYSEMKT:FBTC) down 1.49%. Spot Ether funds also weakened, as iShares Ethereum Trust ETF (NASDAQ:ETHA) fell 3.27%.

Bitcoin's struggle to hold $74,000 raises concerns about the strength of underlying demand. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded approximately $1.5 billion in net outflows since November 2, removing an important source of buying pressure.

Derivatives markets also reflect growing caution. Bitcoin options traders are paying a premium for downside protection, while relatively subdued futures positioning suggests limited appetite for aggressively buying the dip. A recovery in ETF inflows, accompanied by stronger spot buying, would provide a more convincing signal that market conditions are improving.

Altcoins face an even more challenging outlook. Ethereum is approaching the psychologically important $2,000 level, while Solana is testing support near $80. Both could face additional selling pressure if Bitcoin weakens further, particularly as tighter liquidity tends to hit more volatile digital assets hardest.
For now, investors should watch whether Bitcoin can reclaim $75,000 and whether institutional flows begin to stabilize. Without renewed demand, any near-term rebound could prove difficult to sustain.

Cryptocurrency markets took another hit on Tuesday, November 10, as hotter-than-expected inflation data weighed on investor sentiment and fueled concerns about higher interest rates. As of early evening, Bitcoin ( BTC -0.99% ) fell 1.83% to $73,874.38, while Ethereum ( ETH -2.58% ) declined 3.43% to $2,059.16 and Solana ( SOL -2.61% ) dropped 3.69% to $83.37. The broad-based sell-off reflected weakening risk appetite as investors reassessed the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.

Tuesday's inflation surprise triggered a sharp sell-off in U.S. government bonds, pushing Treasury yields higher as investors priced in more aggressive monetary tightening. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield briefly surpassed 5%, while the more policy-sensitive two-year yield climbed toward 4.75%. Higher yields make fixed-income investments more attractive relative to speculative assets, creating additional headwinds for cryptocurrencies.

The U.S. dollar also strengthened, with the dollar index gaining approximately 0.5%. A stronger dollar can weigh on dollar-denominated assets like Bitcoin by tightening global financial conditions and reducing purchasing power for overseas investors.

Meanwhile, markets increasingly expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December, with some traders considering the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point increase. Together, rising bond yields, a stronger dollar, and tighter monetary policy expectations are creating an increasingly challenging backdrop for digital assets.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs traded lower, with iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF ( IBIT -1.51% ) down 1.51% and Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC -1.49% ) down 1.49%. Spot Ether funds also weakened, as iShares Ethereum Trust ETF ( ETHA -3.27% ) fell 3.27%.

Bitcoin's struggle to hold $74,000 raises concerns about the strength of underlying demand. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded approximately $1.5 billion in net outflows since November 2, removing an important source of buying pressure.

Derivatives markets also reflect growing caution. Bitcoin options traders are paying a premium for downside protection, while relatively subdued futures positioning suggests limited appetite for aggressively buying the dip. A recovery in ETF inflows, accompanied by stronger spot buying, would provide a more convincing signal that market conditions are improving.

Altcoins face an even more challenging outlook. Ethereum is approaching the psychologically important $2,000 level, while Solana is testing support near $80. Both could face additional selling pressure if Bitcoin weakens further, particularly as tighter liquidity tends to hit more volatile digital assets hardest.
For now, investors should watch whether Bitcoin can reclaim $75,000 and whether institutional flows begin to stabilize. Without renewed demand, any near-term rebound could prove difficult to sustain.

sources.title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips
passages: Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business.

Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house-developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads.
TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post.
The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote.
The chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can be used to distill and train small models on the fly.
That ability, according to Google, could prove useful for cases where a company might want to train a model on its proprietary data without having to move the data between devices.

extraction.body: Google is notching up its chipmaking game as the company seeks to reduce its dependence on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business. Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units (TPUs), in-house-developed chips meant for AI workloads, that broaden its chip portfolio to additional use cases: confidential inference and more memory capacity for large workloads. The new units, TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the company’s eighth generation of chips introduced in April this year, and build on what those chips offered, which was more inference capacity and support for large training requirements. TPU 8tx, designed with AMD, is based on the TPU 8t chip, and is geared specifically for confidentially training and running AI models, Google said in a blog post. The chip “builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use,” the company wrote. The chip also has a custom inferencing network that lets it run reasoning alongside training, so it can be used to distill and train small models on the fly. That ability, according to Google, could prove useful for cases where a company might want to train a model on its proprietary data without having to move the data between devices. Meanwhile, TPU 8i Max basically combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips the company launched in April, doubling the memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth, but in a single package. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a larger range of information during queries. The chip launch comes as hyperscalers like Microsoft , Amazon , and even AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are working on their own lines of AI-specific semiconductors and accompanying software in order to reduce their reliance on the dominance of Nvidia. The news also comes at a particularly vulnerable moment for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang over the weekend admitted to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy. extraction.body: The Made by Google 2026 lineup is finally complete with tomorrow’s retail launch of the Pixel Tag . You can find our review here , while there are some additional details about the device since the August announcement. The Pixel Tag is the first Find Hub tracker with NFC. Google did not mention this connectivity specification in August, with Near Field Communication letting you tap the tracker to the back of your phone to immediately open device settings. The NFC area on the Pixel Tag is below the circular battery door, which you hold down and twist counterclockwise to open. On Android 17 QPR2, tapping immediately opens the details page. On QPR1, you first get a system notification that you need to click. NFC joins Bluetooth 6.0 with Channel Sounding and Ultra Wideband (UWB). The setup process adds a new screen after the initial pairing and terms of use. It lets you configure: Notify when left behind, Ring this phone, Edit name, Edit category, and Adjust volume for this tag. The Pixel Tag has a physical button on the rear side below the battery cover. Clicking twice plays a loud sound on your phone if both devices are nearby. Once found, you can tap the button once to silence, or turn it off from your phone. This feature can be disabled from the Pixel Tag’s device details page on a tracker-by-tracker basis. Google does not have a first-party case for the Pixel Tag. Instead, it’s working with Made for Google partner Bellroy. There are two models available from the Google Store, with the first made of silicone. The Bellroy Lite Case Duo costs $24.99 and comes in a pack of two: Mist and Shadow colorways. It wraps everything but the face of the Pixel Tag (and its speaker cutout), while giving you a hole in the corner and color-matching cord. There’s also the Bellroy Leather Tag Case in Artichoke, Azalea, Black, Pewter, and Red Ochre for $29.99. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. passages: After years of third-party Android trackers from companies like Samsung, Motorola, and Pebblebee, Google’s Pixel Tag is now available for purchase.
Android phones with a UWB chip can display the exact distance and direction to the Pixel Tag in the Find Hub app once you’re close to it, while Bluetooth Channel Sounding is limited to just distance.

extraction.body: After years of third-party Android trackers from companies like Samsung, Motorola, and Pebblebee, Google’s Pixel Tag is now available for purchase. First announced in August, the Pixel Tag is designed to work with Google’s tracking network and app that was renamed the Find Hub last year. The Pixel Tag is priced similar to Apple’s AirTag 2. A single tracker costs $29.99 while a four-pack is discounted to $99.99. At 0.4 ounces, the Pixel Tag is slightly lighter than the AirTag 2 and while its oblong design is longer than Apple’s tracker, Google’s is a bit thinner. It doesn’t include a hole to attach it to keys, luggage, or other items you want to track, but you can pair it with accessories that make it easy to tether to objects. The tracker also features ultra wideband (UWB) support and Channel Sounding through Bluetooth 6.0. Android phones with a UWB chip can display the exact distance and direction to the Pixel Tag in the Find Hub app once you’re close to it, while Bluetooth Channel Sounding is limited to just distance. The Pixel Tag is compatible with smartphones running Android 9 or later, but you’ll need devices that specifically include a UWB chip or support Bluetooth 6.0 to take advantage of Find Hub’s precise locating features.

extraction.body: After years of third-party Android trackers from companies like Samsung, Motorola, and Pebblebee, Google’s Pixel Tag is now available for purchase. First announced in August, the Pixel Tag is designed to work with Google’s tracking network and app that was renamed the Find Hub last year. The Pixel Tag is priced similar to Apple’s AirTag 2. A single tracker costs $29.99 while a four-pack is discounted to $99.99. At 0.4 ounces, the Pixel Tag is slightly lighter than the AirTag 2 and while its oblong design is longer than Apple’s tracker, Google’s is a bit thinner. It doesn’t include a hole to attach it to keys, luggage, or other items you want to track, but you can pair it with accessories that make it easy to tether to objects. The tracker also features ultra wideband (UWB) support and Channel Sounding through Bluetooth 6.0. Android phones with a UWB chip can display the exact distance and direction to the Pixel Tag in the Find Hub app once you’re close to it, while Bluetooth Channel Sounding is limited to just distance. The Pixel Tag is compatible with smartphones running Android 9 or later, but you’ll need devices that specifically include a UWB chip or support Bluetooth 6.0 to take advantage of Find Hub’s precise locating features.

passages: MELBOURNE, Australia -- Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by a rogue OpenAI agent in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday.
The proposed AI regulator would follow Australia appointing an eSafety Commissioner in 2015.
The office describes itself as the world’s first government agency dedicated to keeping people safer online.
The regulator would enforce world-leading legislated AI standards that would apply to all frontier AI companies that want to operate in Australia, Albanese said.
Financial penalties would apply, although the government has yet to detail those penalties.
OpenAI apologized in September for the breach and its slow response.
“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement.
“We also should have handled our response better.”
A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations including that the government consider changing the law.
“The point is law needs to get ahead of and in some cases make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world.
And to be clear, Australia is a first-mover in these areas,” Albanese said.

“When it comes to the generational opportunity that artificial intelligence offers Australia, I’ve been very clear: our task is to make sure we shape AI rather than AI shape us,” Albanese told reporters.
It is not clear whether the portal breach broke any Australian laws.

sources.title: Amazon's Ring launches flying security drones, patrol robots to guard homes, businesses
passages: Amazon introduced an indoor security drone made by Ring, offering a flying camera to monitor areas stationary devices cannot reach, the company announced Tuesday.

It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have." The $250 indoor drone allows users to set automated patrol routes on a schedule or deploy the device on demand.  AMAZON CRASH ATTORNEYS SAY PILOT PAIRING MAY HAVE BEEN KEY FLAW BEHIND FATAL INCIDENT When a connected Ring camera, sensor, or alarm is triggered, the drone automatically flies to designated patrol points to investigate.  It features a 148-degree field of view, 360-degree rotation, and dual built-in LED lights for low-light environments.
The company also unveiled the Ring Rover Cam, an autonomous security robot for businesses that patrols, investigates disturbances, and streams up to 4K video.

"For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one," said Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff.  AMAZON TO CUT NEARLY 1,000 WHITE-COLLAR JOBS ACROSS STORES DIVISION AND OTHER UNITS: REPORT "The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be," he added.

sources.title: Amazon’s Ring debuts security robots, including a drone
passages: Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where fixed cameras cannot reach.

It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.” The drone provides “wall-to-wall coverage,” according to Ring, with 148-degree peripheral vision and the ability to rotate 360 degrees to quickly spot potential threats.
“Privacy isn’t just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default,” Ring said in explaining privacy safeguards.
“And you’ll always know when the devices are recording,” Ring said.
The $250 Ring Drone Camera offers exactly what the product’s name implies — the technology to capture moving images from a lens affixed to a small quadcopter drone, according to the company.
Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff said his customers have been asking for an expansion of the company’s popular doorbell cameras without having to install more cameras around the home.
Ring also rolled out its $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, tailored for businesses.
“Both devices are built to deter, not just monitor.” Ring, in its sales pitch, directly took on concerns about bringing such technology behind closed doors.

extraction.body: Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where fixed cameras cannot reach. The $250 Ring Drone Camera offers exactly what the product’s name implies — the technology to capture moving images from a lens affixed to a small quadcopter drone, according to the company. Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff said his customers have been asking for an expansion of the company’s popular doorbell cameras without having to install more cameras around the home. “For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one,” Siminoff said in a statement the company released Tuesday. “The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be. But we kept at it until we got it right—and that’s Ring Robotics. It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.” The drone provides “wall-to-wall coverage,” according to Ring, with 148-degree peripheral vision and the ability to rotate 360 degrees to quickly spot potential threats. LED lights also equip it to work in “low-light environments” so homeowners can “always get clear, crisp video,” the company said. Ring also rolled out its $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, tailored for businesses. The tool could be used to “investigate a disturbance” or be set to do “regular sweeps” of a property. “Get a closer look wherever and whenever you need it without the cost and complexity of wiring up every corner of every room,” the company said. The devices are not quiet by design, Ring said, with drone propellers easily heard and the robot featuring a “light tower” that is “bright and easy to spot.” “If someone’s there who shouldn’t be, a flying drone overhead or a roving robot with a siren makes it clear they’ve been spotted,” the company said. “Both devices are built to deter, not just monitor.” Ring, in its sales pitch, directly took on concerns about bringing such technology behind closed doors. “Privacy isn’t just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default,” Ring said in explaining privacy safeguards. It assured consumers that cameras and recording features will be off when the drone isn’t flying or when the rover is in sleep mode. “And you’ll always know when the devices are recording,” Ring said. “Both have LED indicators, and Ring Rover tells you right on its screen.” But Michelle Dahl, a civil rights attorney and executive director of the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, a privacy advocacy group, urged consumers to think twice before they invite recording devices into their homes. “When you are allowing cameras within your own home, there is a really big risk of a data breach,” she told NBC News. “It’s a bizarre thing to introduce to the market when you consider all the issues it poses.” Both pieces of equipment require a subscription fee of $5 per month or $60 annually, a customer service rep said.

sources.title: Amazon’s Ring debuts security robots, including a drone
passages: Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where fixed cameras cannot reach.

It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.” The drone provides “wall-to-wall coverage,” according to Ring, with 148-degree peripheral vision and the ability to rotate 360 degrees to quickly spot potential threats.
“Privacy isn’t just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default,” Ring said in explaining privacy safeguards.
“And you’ll always know when the devices are recording,” Ring said.
The $250 Ring Drone Camera offers exactly what the product’s name implies — the technology to capture moving images from a lens affixed to a small quadcopter drone, according to the company.
Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff said his customers have been asking for an expansion of the company’s popular doorbell cameras without having to install more cameras around the home.
Ring also rolled out its $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, tailored for businesses.
“Both devices are built to deter, not just monitor.” Ring, in its sales pitch, directly took on concerns about bringing such technology behind closed doors.

extraction.body: Amazon’s Ring has launched an indoor security drone, the company said Tuesday, offering homeowners room-to-room surveillance where fixed cameras cannot reach. The $250 Ring Drone Camera offers exactly what the product’s name implies — the technology to capture moving images from a lens affixed to a small quadcopter drone, according to the company. Ring founder and chief inventor Jamie Siminoff said his customers have been asking for an expansion of the company’s popular doorbell cameras without having to install more cameras around the home. “For years, customers told us they wanted eyes in the places a fixed camera couldn’t reach, and peace of mind in the spots they’d never want one,” Siminoff said in a statement the company released Tuesday. “The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be. But we kept at it until we got it right—and that’s Ring Robotics. It’s not just a new category of security; it’s the beginning of a future where proactive, autonomous protection is something every home and every business can have.” The drone provides “wall-to-wall coverage,” according to Ring, with 148-degree peripheral vision and the ability to rotate 360 degrees to quickly spot potential threats. LED lights also equip it to work in “low-light environments” so homeowners can “always get clear, crisp video,” the company said. Ring also rolled out its $1,000 Ring Rover Cam, tailored for businesses. The tool could be used to “investigate a disturbance” or be set to do “regular sweeps” of a property. “Get a closer look wherever and whenever you need it without the cost and complexity of wiring up every corner of every room,” the company said. The devices are not quiet by design, Ring said, with drone propellers easily heard and the robot featuring a “light tower” that is “bright and easy to spot.” “If someone’s there who shouldn’t be, a flying drone overhead or a roving robot with a siren makes it clear they’ve been spotted,” the company said. “Both devices are built to deter, not just monitor.” Ring, in its sales pitch, directly took on concerns about bringing such technology behind closed doors. “Privacy isn’t just a feature of Ring Robotics; it is the default,” Ring said in explaining privacy safeguards. It assured consumers that cameras and recording features will be off when the drone isn’t flying or when the rover is in sleep mode. “And you’ll always know when the devices are recording,” Ring said. “Both have LED indicators, and Ring Rover tells you right on its screen.” But Michelle Dahl, a civil rights attorney and executive director of the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, a privacy advocacy group, urged consumers to think twice before they invite recording devices into their homes. “When you are allowing cameras within your own home, there is a really big risk of a data breach,” she told NBC News. “It’s a bizarre thing to introduce to the market when you consider all the issues it poses.” Both pieces of equipment require a subscription fee of $5 per month or $60 annually, a customer service rep said.

sources.title: Celeste Kirschner, CAE, MHSA, on current issues facing independent urology practices
passages: In an interview at the 2025 LUGPA Annual Meeting, LUGPA CEO Celeste Kirschner, CAE, MHSA, sat down with Urology Times® to outline the biggest challenges facing independent urology practices today.
Kirschner began the discussion by highlighting 2 pressing issues facing urology practices: declining physician payment rates amid rising inflation and the need for PBM reform.

Beyond advocacy, Kirschner also discussed how urology groups are leveraging data analytics and exploring emerging technologies like artificial intelligence to improve practice efficiency and patient care.
She pointed to initiatives such as the LUGPA playbook and practice data projects, which are helping members understand how best to use these tools in clinical practice.

extraction.body: At the LUGPA Annual Meeting in Chicago, a panel discussed how they are currently using artificial intelligence (AI) at their urology practices. Jared Olafsson, Alexander Epelbaum, MD, and Daoud Dajani, MD, each presented their experiences. Ambient scribes, which listen to conversations between clinicians and patients and provide structured clinical notes, can save physicians hours of manual documentation. Lowering the documentation burden also reduces burnout and dissatisfaction. Some current ambient scribe platforms can even generate clinical suggestions, such as diagnosis code recommendations, and post orders in the electronic medical record. Dr Epelbaum, market president at Integrated Medical Professionals and a practicing urologist, has been instrumental in bringing ambient documentation into daily clinic work. “You kind of want AI to be your silent partner working in the background, not interfering with the physicians or any clinicians’ workflows,” he said. Recently, Dr Epelbaum moved from a pilot phase to launching ambient scribe technology for the entire New York market. “Over the last 3 months, we have generated 44,000 notes with over 4000 hours of transcription time,” Dr Epelbaum said. Clinicians are still responsible for the content and accuracy of the notes, however. “If you didn’t say it, it didn’t happen. AI cannot make assumptions, so you need to explicitly say everything that you’re taking the patient through,” Dr Epelbaum said. Over the last several months, the possibilities for AI applications have grown immensely. “It has evolved from simple one-task solutions to now being able to dictate something to AI and having it autonomously build it for you,” said Olafsson, business operations manager at Urology San Antonio in Texas. He described using Claude Code to build a physician call schedule manager that analyzes the fairness of the call schedule with historical holiday and weekend data. “AI is super effective when 2 conditions are met: when the field is data rich and when it is really rules based,” Olafsson said. Currently, Olafsson uses agentic AI in the call center via speech-to-speech models. “We put an agent at the front of the tree where you know every call is able to be answered immediately. Then it routes through that tree and ends up at the right place at the right time,” Olafsson said. For callers, agentic AI might also reduce time spent and frustration from navigating different levels of phone trees. Because AI capabilities are evolving so quickly, increasing capacity by 2 to 3 times every 6 months, Olafsson advised against signing long-term technology tool agreements spanning several years. Olafsson also cautioned against moving too quickly. “We want to make sure we clearly understand the problem before seeking a solution.” Dr Dajani, chief medical officer at Chesapeake Urology in Maryland, remarked that he uses AI to generate feedback and suggestions for clinic staff. In his practice, he used Replit to develop a platform that analyzes patient survey data, identifies themes, and provides staff with tailored advice on how to improve. Across the panel, the use of AI for revenue cycle management sparked interest. In the next couple of years, AI could manage coding, identify denial patterns, manage automatic denial letters, and autonomously handle prior authorization requests by scrubbing patient records and communicating with insurance companies via AI agents. If this pans out, the time to go through the prior authorization process would plummet from weeks to just a few minutes. extraction.body: At the LUGPA Annual Meeting in Chicago, a panel discussed how they are currently using artificial intelligence (AI) at their urology practices. Jared Olafsson, Alexander Epelbaum, MD, and Daoud Dajani, MD, each presented their experiences. Ambient scribes, which listen to conversations between clinicians and patients and provide structured clinical notes, can save physicians hours of manual documentation. Lowering the documentation burden also reduces burnout and dissatisfaction. Some current ambient scribe platforms can even generate clinical suggestions, such as diagnosis code recommendations, and post orders in the electronic medical record. Dr Epelbaum, market president at Integrated Medical Professionals and a practicing urologist, has been instrumental in bringing ambient documentation into daily clinic work. “You kind of want AI to be your silent partner working in the background, not interfering with the physicians or any clinicians’ workflows,” he said. Recently, Dr Epelbaum moved from a pilot phase to launching ambient scribe technology for the entire New York market. “Over the last 3 months, we have generated 44,000 notes with over 4000 hours of transcription time,” Dr Epelbaum said. Clinicians are still responsible for the content and accuracy of the notes, however. “If you didn’t say it, it didn’t happen. AI cannot make assumptions, so you need to explicitly say everything that you’re taking the patient through,” Dr Epelbaum said. Over the last several months, the possibilities for AI applications have grown immensely. “It has evolved from simple one-task solutions to now being able to dictate something to AI and having it autonomously build it for you,” said Olafsson, business operations manager at Urology San Antonio in Texas. He described using Claude Code to build a physician call schedule manager that analyzes the fairness of the call schedule with historical holiday and weekend data. “AI is super effective when 2 conditions are met: when the field is data rich and when it is really rules based,” Olafsson said. Currently, Olafsson uses agentic AI in the call center via speech-to-speech models. “We put an agent at the front of the tree where you know every call is able to be answered immediately. Then it routes through that tree and ends up at the right place at the right time,” Olafsson said. For callers, agentic AI might also reduce time spent and frustration from navigating different levels of phone trees. Because AI capabilities are evolving so quickly, increasing capacity by 2 to 3 times every 6 months, Olafsson advised against signing long-term technology tool agreements spanning several years. Olafsson also cautioned against moving too quickly. “We want to make sure we clearly understand the problem before seeking a solution.” Dr Dajani, chief medical officer at Chesapeake Urology in Maryland, remarked that he uses AI to generate feedback and suggestions for clinic staff. In his practice, he used Replit to develop a platform that analyzes patient survey data, identifies themes, and provides staff with tailored advice on how to improve. Across the panel, the use of AI for revenue cycle management sparked interest. In the next couple of years, AI could manage coding, identify denial patterns, manage automatic denial letters, and autonomously handle prior authorization requests by scrubbing patient records and communicating with insurance companies via AI agents. If this pans out, the time to go through the prior authorization process would plummet from weeks to just a few minutes. sources.title: The war-induced exodus from Russia: A security problem or a convenient political bogey? - FIIA - Finnish Institute of International Affairs
passages: Frontpage / Publications / The war-induced exodus from Russia: A security problem or a conv ...
The exodus of Russians after 24 February 2022 has had a tangible socio-economic impact on receiving states, predominantly the countries of Central Asia, Georgia, and Turkey.

Approximately 800,000 Russians have left their homeland so far due to the war in Ukraine, and in particular due to the "partial military mobilization" announced on 21 September 2022. [1] Although the majority of EU member states continued to issue visas for Russian citizens, including for tourism purposes, several countries sealed their borders to Russian tourists after the announcement.
Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland banned leisure travel from Russia in early September 2022, and Finland joined them on 30 September.
The political leadership of these countries insisted that travel is a privilege and not a human right.
The major argument for denying Russians the right to cross the EU borders was ethical, pointing out that tourism during wartime is not appropriate.

Yet other grounds mostly dealt with potential security threats, namely the likelihood of espionage, intelligence gathering, proliferation of potential saboteurs, as well as fears of Russian retaliation. [2]
The paper begins by considering the rhetoric of securitization around Russian migrants.

It then discusses the attitudes and political behaviour of migrants in receiving states, concluding that seeing migrants as a potential source of change is more fruitful than excessive politicization of the issue.
Despite the tightening of migration legislation even in visa-free countries, Russian migrants have succeeded in creating civic networks and organizations in the receiving countries.
They cover a variety of functions from private schooling and psychotherapy to civic education and political activism.
Migrants do not trust the Russian government and less than 1% said they had voted for the United Russia party.
Migrants are extremely active politically and willing to maintain horizontal networks.
Interest in political life in Russia often goes hand in hand with a growing interest in their new country's politics.
More than half of the respondents were interested in the politics of the country where they found themselves at the time of the survey.
Finnish Institute of International Affairs Arkadiankatu 23 B FI-00100 Helsinki

One opinion poll found that as many as 69% of respondents in Georgia believe that Georgia should introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens, and 57% consider the Georgian authorities' approach to the entry of Russian citizens unacceptable. [7] It cannot be ruled out that the Georgian political leadership may eventually be receptive to such demands, although President Salome Zourabichvili does not deem the Russian migrants – including draft evaders – a security threat.
While Russian emigration is significantly less numerous than the influx of those fleeing the war, its scale deserves additional scrutiny as it entails multiple implications for receiving countries.
Yet this does not necessarily mean that these communities are ineffective in bringing about change in Russian domestic politics.
Those who find themselves in democratic countries can gain practical skills and grow networks beyond Russian-speaking associations.
They also maintain close ties with those in Russia and provide access to uncensored political information.
For example, the Latvian Foreign Minister, Edgars Rinkevics, considered fleeing Russians to be a "counterintelligence risk" as agents for potential covert operations could sneak in among them.

Historical traumas of Russian occupation have become re-politicized during the war and have also played a role in galvanizing the question of Russian minorities and Russian travellers during electoral campaigns in Estonia and Latvia.
For example, Georgia lost control over parts of its internationally recognized territory after Russia recognized the independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia.
These circumstances give the government in Tbilisi additional incentives to hedge against new political risks.
For instance, Georgia denies right of entry to some outspoken Russian oppositionists.

Other post-Soviet states also pursue a risk-averse strategy in handling communications with the Kremlin while continuing to accommodate Russian draft evaders, IT specialists, and political opposition.
The data on trust dynamics among migrants clearly shows that the degree of trust in fellow émigrés is enormous and amounts to more than 90% (see Figure 2).
Trust in receiving societies among Russian migrants also remains high (80–81%).
The increased likelihood of cross-border repression calls for a more consistent response and policies toward political migrants.
Offering humanitarian visas would be a flexible and less costly tool to provide political activists with access to proper protection.
Asylum decisions should always be based on objective criteria and individual assessments.

Understandably, war refugees must be the priority; however, support for Ukrainian war refugees and Russian political refugees must not be viewed as 'a zero-sum game', where assisting one group rules out helping the other.
According to a panel survey, Russian war-induced migrants also engage in charity activities and volunteer work.
There was a significant increase in volunteering, from 15.7% in March 2022 to almost 22% in the autumn.

A growing negative attitude towards Russia as an aggressor state had spillover effects on Russian speakers in general, irrespective of their political leanings, including those prosecuted by the Russian state.
Leisure travellers and political émigrés constitute different categories and must be treated differently.
International humanitarian law protects persons who suffer threats from their governments or para-governmental organizations.
To preserve what remains of civil society infrastructure and networks in Russia, a more flexible approach by the EU and Finland towards Russian migrants would be more valid.
It is also worth mentioning that most Schengen tourist visas expired during the Covid-19 pandemic.

In addition, people were aware of the high cost of living in Europe and of the fact that the mobilization in Russia could become a tipping point for some EU countries to begin to revise their migration regulations.

In another social media post, he elaborated that "in times of war there have always been special rules and quiet groups of impeccably inconspicuous people who effectively enforce them". [6] Such messages clearly signal that crossing the Russian border does not mean being in a safe place.
Certain activities by Russian emigrants have been successfully institutionalized into transnational networks uniting hundreds of communities around the globe.
One of the networks that aids Russians in moving and settling into new countries is Kovcheg (The Ark).
The organization explicitly limits its assistance to those who share the anti-war stance and, in addition to legal and logistical assistance, organizes lectures and events of a political nature.
The organization's founder, Anastasia Burakova, has been labelled as a foreign agent in Russia.

Another organization, Idite lesom (a play on words that means both 'escape through the forest' and 'go to hell'), provides advice and offers safe routes to draft evaders, including professional military servicemen.

In this context it is worth recalling that in August 2022, Finland’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Pekka Haavisto, announced an intention to grant humanitarian visas, although the procedure is still not available for applicants.

extraction.body: Frontpage / Publications / The war-induced exodus from Russia: A security problem or a conv ... With an increasing probability of cross-border repression – persecution or intimidation of political migrants abroad – it is essential that the EU adopts a consistent response towards political migrants, including those from Russia. The war in Ukraine has produced the largest number of refugees in the European Union since the Second World War. The full-scale invasion of Ukraine has also resulted in a large exodus of people from Russia, which poses tangible socio-economic and infrastructural challenges to receiving societies within the EU and beyond. While Russian emigration is significantly less numerous than the influx of those fleeing the war, its scale deserves additional scrutiny as it entails multiple implications for receiving countries. Approximately 800,000 Russians have left their homeland so far due to the war in Ukraine, and in particular due to the "partial military mobilization" announced on 21 September 2022. [1] Although the majority of EU member states continued to issue visas for Russian citizens, including for tourism purposes, several countries sealed their borders to Russian tourists after the announcement. Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland banned leisure travel from Russia in early September 2022, and Finland joined them on 30 September. The political leadership of these countries insisted that travel is a privilege and not a human right. The major argument for denying Russians the right to cross the EU borders was ethical, pointing out that tourism during wartime is not appropriate. Yet other grounds mostly dealt with potential security threats, namely the likelihood of espionage, intelligence gathering, proliferation of potential saboteurs, as well as fears of Russian retaliation. [2] Indeed, the influx of Russian migrants created tensions at the Georgian border and congested the Russian-Finnish border in late September. On the other hand, even before Russia’s western land borders were closed, the majority of migrants preferred the post-Soviet countries – Kazakhstan, Armenia, and Georgia – due to the visa-free entry and convenient transport connections. It is also worth mentioning that most Schengen tourist visas expired during the Covid-19 pandemic. In addition, people were aware of the high cost of living in Europe and of the fact that the mobilization in Russia could become a tipping point for some EU countries to begin to revise their migration regulations. This Briefing Paper argues that the recent war-induced migration from Russia is unlikely to pose any major security threat to receiving states, although it has created challenges for them in terms of social security, real estate, and labour markets. The political impact on the receiving states has remained and will remain limited. The paper begins by considering the rhetoric of securitization around Russian migrants. It then discusses the attitudes and political behaviour of migrants in receiving states, concluding that seeing migrants as a potential source of change is more fruitful than excessive politicization of the issue. According to the official statistics provided by receiving states, the number of war-induced Russian migrants that landed in the EU in 2022 is relatively small – 36,282 persons, while the post-Soviet countries and Turkey accepted an unprecedented number of incoming migrants. Most of the migrants ended up in Kazakhstan (146,000), Turkey (78,998), Georgia (60,000), and Armenia (42,000) (see Figure 1). [3] For example, the small state of Israel accommodated roughly the same number of Russian émigrés as the whole EU, and this figure does not even include those who were already in possession of Israeli passports but have only left Russia now. According to a panel survey conducted by the OutRush research group in spring and autumn 2022, the choice of countries was mostly random and depended on airfare availability and entry regulations: 58% of the migrant respondents in spring 2022 confirmed that the choice of destination was random, 32% went to countries where their relatives or friends already lived, 13% were well acquainted with the culture of the receiving country, and 10% were relocated by their employer or went through programmes of international assistance (e.g., Scholars at Risk). For many, these countries turned out to be the final destination, but about a quarter continued their journey. According to the same survey, 56% stated that it is very likely that they will stay in their current countries. [4] That said, the EU states did not experience (and are unlikely to experience in the future) a dramatic surge in Russian migrants even before the visa bans and the border closures. Yet Russian migrants became an overly politicized issue in certain EU member states. The potential security risks associated with Russian migrants are viewed as higher in the states that border Russia. For example, the Latvian Foreign Minister, Edgars Rinkevics, considered fleeing Russians to be a "counterintelligence risk" as agents for potential covert operations could sneak in among them. His Estonian counterpart, Urmas Reinsalu, expressed similar concerns, referring to the Russian security service operatives who entered Ukraine on the eve of the annexation in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. He also claimed that "many of the operatives of [the] Russian security services responsible for poisonings, explosions, et cetera, used tourist visas and false identities". [5] There were even more radical statements of the kind that Russian émigrés could be instrumentalized and weaponized as a hybrid threat akin to the crisis at the Belarusian-Polish border in 2021. Historical traumas of Russian occupation have become re-politicized during the war and have also played a role in galvanizing the question of Russian minorities and Russian travellers during electoral campaigns in Estonia and Latvia. A growing negative attitude towards Russia as an aggressor state had spillover effects on Russian speakers in general, irrespective of their political leanings, including those prosecuted by the Russian state. However, excessive politicization of incoming Russian migrants does more harm than good. Leisure travellers and political émigrés constitute different categories and must be treated differently. International humanitarian law protects persons who suffer threats from their governments or para-governmental organizations. Apart from those who face intimidation by the state, there are civil society activists, professional oppositionists, educators, and journalists who constitute the backbone of political resistance and thus bear disproportionate political risks compared to the rest of the Russian population. To preserve what remains of civil society infrastructure and networks in Russia, a more flexible approach by the EU and Finland towards Russian migrants would be more valid. In February 2022, Dmitry Medvedev, Deputy Head of the Russian Security Council, referred to recent migrants who spoke out as "traitors who have gone over to the enemy and want their Fatherland to perish". In another social media post, he elaborated that "in times of war there have always been special rules and quiet groups of impeccably inconspicuous people who effectively enforce them". [6] Such messages clearly signal that crossing the Russian border does not mean being in a safe place. Cross-border or transnational repression – persecution or intimidation of political migrants abroad – has become a new challenge for Russians in exile. So far, Russian ex-territorial operations by the secret services have been limited to poisonings and mysterious deaths of certain businessmen abroad. Nevertheless, cross-border repression of political dissidents implemented by authoritarian states is not unheard of. No longer does President Putin refer to emigration as a de-toxification of Russian society; political migrants are seen as traitors, and therefore as objects of intimidation and prosecution. Thus, the danger is real and must be considered by the receiving states according to international humanitarian law. So while it is unsurprising that precisely those EU member states that border Russia do not offer humanitarian visas and refuse to distinguish between regime opponents, economic migrants, and tourists, a more nuanced approach would be appropriate and is, in fact, overdue. In this context it is worth recalling that in August 2022, Finland’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Pekka Haavisto, announced an intention to grant humanitarian visas, although the procedure is still not available for applicants. The nature of security threats for the post-Soviet countries differs from that faced by EU states or Turkey and stems from closer ties with Russia, weaker military capacity, as well as perceptions of historical legacy linked to Russia. For example, Georgia lost control over parts of its internationally recognized territory after Russia recognized the independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia. These circumstances give the government in Tbilisi additional incentives to hedge against new political risks. For instance, Georgia denies right of entry to some outspoken Russian oppositionists. Other post-Soviet states also pursue a risk-averse strategy in handling communications with the Kremlin while continuing to accommodate Russian draft evaders, IT specialists, and political opposition. So far, there are very few cases of extradition or denial of entry, but at the same time, the logic of political risk-aversion suggests that Russian oppositionists are not entirely safe in these states. All states tend to welcome economic Russian migration, but this does not mean that they offer opportunities for civic and political activism. The nature of the political regimes in receiving countries does play a role in how a government reacts to the incoming migrants from Russia. One opinion poll found that as many as 69% of respondents in Georgia believe that Georgia should introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens, and 57% consider the Georgian authorities' approach to the entry of Russian citizens unacceptable. [7] It cannot be ruled out that the Georgian political leadership may eventually be receptive to such demands, although President Salome Zourabichvili does not deem the Russian migrants – including draft evaders – a security threat. For many, these countries turned out to be the final destination, but about a quarter continued their journey. According to the same survey, 56% stated that it is very likely that they will stay in their current countries. Instead, users encounter state outlets such as RT and Sputnik , which flood feeds with official updates and interviews with generals. Alongside them are grassroots volunteers, war correspondents ( voenkory ) and military bloggers (“milbloggers”), who use these platforms to organise activities and share updates from the frontlines. VKontakte (VK), one of the country’s largest social networks, has more than 90 million monthly users , while Odnoklassniki, popular with older Russians , has around 34.2 million . As of 2024, 51 per cent of Russians used Telegram , and many reportedly continue to access it despite the nationwide block imposed in April 2026 . For many users, the war is less something they follow through formal news than something they encounter constantly on these platforms. This shift accelerated after social media sites like Facebook and Instagram were banned following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, pushing users toward domestic platforms. As of 2025, Russia had around 106 million social media user identities , roughly 74 per cent of the population. Platforms such as VK and RuTube have grown in prominence, as has Dzen (formerly Yandex Zen), a longer-form blogging and news aggregation platform VK acquired from Yandex in 2022 . Users rarely rely on a single platform. They check updates in one place, follow discussions in another and read longer interpretations elsewhere. Some still access banned Western platforms , staying connected to the wider world and posting Russian perspectives there. Bots and channels promoting state positions and views also play a major part in this ecosystem. Telegram channels play a particularly important role. Nearly half of Russians read Telegram news channels at least weekly, even after the block. Channels such as Rybar , which specialises in maps and analysis, and WarGonzo, run by war correspondent Semyon Pegov, publish battlefield reports and commentary that users return to throughout the day. Research suggests Telegram has become one of the key spaces for political communication during the war. This habit of constant checking means that, for many users, the conflict can feel less like distant news than an event followed in near real time. Repeated exposure also shapes how opinions develop. Platform algorithms are not neutral: if users repeatedly view certain types of content, recommendation systems such as VK’s make similar content more visible in their feeds. Understanding is not formed instantly but built through repetition, and when similar narratives appear many times a day, they begin to feel true . Comment sections illustrate this. Many responses are short and almost automatic, with some users simply signalling their presence, while others question information in detail or compare channels. This does not mean users do not think critically, but it suggests that familiarity often substitutes for verification. Military bloggers add another layer. Their posts are direct and emotive, and are widely shared across Telegram. Studies show the number of such bloggers and influencers grew during key phases of the war. Their posts generate large discussions in which users agree, question and argue with one another, but these disagreements largely take place within the information environment users already inhabit. People are engaging actively without necessarily stepping outside it. Age tends to shape these patterns. Russians aged 18–34 are more likely to use social media and Telegram for news, while older Russians rely mostly on state media. Younger users also use these platforms to discuss the war, process information about it and question it. Because content circulates across Telegram, VK and other spaces, research shows these platforms form overlapping discussion spaces, and responses within them are far from uniform , ranging from concern and support to fatigue. Hashtags shape how people express themselves online. Phrases such as #МыВместе ( #MyVmeste , “We are together”) and #СвоихНеБросаем ( #SvoikhNeBrosaem , “We don’t abandon our own”) recur across posts and, over time, carry a shared meaning . Users do not just read them; they reuse them as a simple signal of alignment. Visual content reinforces this. Studies indicate that images and videos, especially of conflict scenes, have played a critical role in constructing Russian identity during the war, amplified by social media echo chambers. Such content provokes pride, support or concern, fuelling nationalist sentiment and a sense of togetherness that mobilises support for the war. Social media is also used to raise donations for military equipment and to organise volunteer activities. Taking part builds networks of collective action and strengthens ties between participants . Regional patterns differ. In Belgorod, on the border with Ukraine, local VK groups centre on everyday life , with residents discussing drone attacks and how the war has changed their lives. These groups help locals coordinate and share updates, but they also bring the conflict closer to users across Russia’s vast territory, making it feel more immediate. The result is neither complete acceptance nor full scepticism, but something in between. Opinions form gradually, less through deliberate choices than through repeated exposure, interaction and everyday engagement. Russia’s online space is neither fully controlled nor fully open. This matters for outside observers. Headline polling on “support” for the war captures only part of the picture. Efforts to reach Russian audiences with alternative information will struggle if they treat Russians as people who simply accept the information presented to them or critics waiting for the facts. In Russia’s digital ecosystem, opinion is shaped by habit and belonging as much as by belief. Her research focuses on indigenous community governance in the Arctic with a broader interest in climate change, environmental governance, governance and policy making, and Russian Foreign Policy. coreStoryFacts.text: Frontpage / Publications / The war-induced exodus from Russia: A security problem or a conv ...
The exodus of Russians after 24 February 2022 has had a tangible socio-economic impact on receiving states, predominantly the countries of Central Asia, Georgia, and Turkey.

Approximately 800,000 Russians have left their homeland so far due to the war in Ukraine, and in particular due to the "partial military mobilization" announced on 21 September 2022. [1] Although the majority of EU member states continued to issue visas for Russian citizens, including for tourism purposes, several countries sealed their borders to Russian tourists after the announcement.
Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland banned leisure travel from Russia in early September 2022, and Finland joined them on 30 September.
The political leadership of these countries insisted that travel is a privilege and not a human right.
The major argument for denying Russians the right to cross the EU borders was ethical, pointing out that tourism during wartime is not appropriate.

Yet other grounds mostly dealt with potential security threats, namely the likelihood of espionage, intelligence gathering, proliferation of potential saboteurs, as well as fears of Russian retaliation. [2]
The paper begins by considering the rhetoric of securitization around Russian migrants.

It then discusses the attitudes and political behaviour of migrants in receiving states, concluding that seeing migrants as a potential source of change is more fruitful than excessive politicization of the issue.
Despite the tightening of migration legislation even in visa-free countries, Russian migrants have succeeded in creating civic networks and organizations in the receiving countries.
They cover a variety of functions from private schooling and psychotherapy to civic education and political activism.
Migrants do not trust the Russian government and less than 1% said they had voted for the United Russia party.
Migrants are extremely active politically and willing to maintain horizontal networks.
Interest in political life in Russia often goes hand in hand with a growing interest in their new country's politics.
More than half of the respondents were interested in the politics of the country where they found themselves at the time of the survey.
Finnish Institute of International Affairs Arkadiankatu 23 B FI-00100 Helsinki

One opinion poll found that as many as 69% of respondents in Georgia believe that Georgia should introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens, and 57% consider the Georgian authorities' approach to the entry of Russian citizens unacceptable. [7] It cannot be ruled out that the Georgian political leadership may eventually be receptive to such demands, although President Salome Zourabichvili does not deem the Russian migrants – including draft evaders – a security threat.
While Russian emigration is significantly less numerous than the influx of those fleeing the war, its scale deserves additional scrutiny as it entails multiple implications for receiving countries.
Yet this does not necessarily mean that these communities are ineffective in bringing about change in Russian domestic politics.
Those who find themselves in democratic countries can gain practical skills and grow networks beyond Russian-speaking associations.
They also maintain close ties with those in Russia and provide access to uncensored political information.
For example, the Latvian Foreign Minister, Edgars Rinkevics, considered fleeing Russians to be a "counterintelligence risk" as agents for potential covert operations could sneak in among them.

Historical traumas of Russian occupation have become re-politicized during the war and have also played a role in galvanizing the question of Russian minorities and Russian travellers during electoral campaigns in Estonia and Latvia.
For example, Georgia lost control over parts of its internationally recognized territory after Russia recognized the independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia.

These circumstances give the government in Tbilisi additional incentives to hedge against new political risks.

In addition, people were aware of the high cost of living in Europe and of the fact that the mobilization in Russia could become a tipping point for some EU countries to begin to revise their migration regulations.

In another social media post, he elaborated that "in times of war there have always been special rules and quiet groups of impeccably inconspicuous people who effectively enforce them". [6] Such messages clearly signal that crossing the Russian border does not mean being in a safe place.
Certain activities by Russian emigrants have been successfully institutionalized into transnational networks uniting hundreds of communities around the globe.
One of the networks that aids Russians in moving and settling into new countries is Kovcheg (The Ark).
The organization explicitly limits its assistance to those who share the anti-war stance and, in addition to legal and logistical assistance, organizes lectures and events of a political nature.
The organization's founder, Anastasia Burakova, has been labelled as a foreign agent in Russia.

Another organization, Idite lesom (a play on words that means both 'escape through the forest' and 'go to hell'), provides advice and offers safe routes to draft evaders, including professional military servicemen.

In this context it is worth recalling that in August 2022, Finland’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Pekka Haavisto, announced an intention to grant humanitarian visas, although the procedure is still not available for applicants.
